questions.title: Streaming Triggers
questions.question: A streaming job processes data from a message queue. The business requires the job to process all available data once per hour and then stop. Which trigger configuration should be used?

choices.A: `trigger(processingTime='1 hour')`
choices.B: `trigger(once=True)`
choices.C: `trigger(availableNow=True)`
choices.D: `trigger(continuous='1 hour')`

questions.shortAnswer: `availableNow=True` processes all available data and stops, making it ideal for scheduled batch-like streaming. `processingTime` runs continuously. `once=True` is deprecated and only processes one batch. `continuous` is for low-latency and doesn't stop.

questions.title: Watermarking in Streaming
questions.question: A streaming aggregation job groups events by a 10-minute window. Events can arrive up to 30 minutes late. Which watermark configuration is correct?

choices.A: `withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")`
choices.B: `withWatermark("event_time", "30 minutes")`
choices.C: `withWatermark("event_time", "40 minutes")`
choices.D: `withWatermark("processing_time", "30 minutes")`

questions.shortAnswer: The watermark should match the maximum expected lateness (30 minutes). This tells Spark to wait 30 minutes before finalizing windows. Using event_time (not processing_time) is required for event-time processing.

questions.title: Incremental Processing with readStream
questions.question: A pipeline reads from a Delta table that receives both inserts and updates. Only new and updated records should be processed. Which configuration enables this?

choices.A: `spark.readStream.option("ignoreChanges", "true").table("source")`
choices.B: `spark.readStream.option("readChangeData", "true").table("source")`
choices.C: `spark.readStream.option("readChangeFeed", "true").table("source")`
choices.D: `spark.readStream.option("skipChangeCommits", "true").table("source")`

questions.shortAnswer: `readChangeFeed = true` (with CDF enabled on the table) reads the change data feed which includes inserts, updates, and deletes. Option A ignores updates/deletes. Option B uses the wrong option name (`readChangeData` is not valid; the correct name is `readChangeFeed`). Option D is not a valid option.

questions.title: Stream-Stream Join
questions.question: A data engineer needs to join two streaming sources - clickstream events and ad impressions - to calculate ad conversion rates. Both streams have event timestamps. What is required when performing a stream-stream join?

choices.A: Both streams must use the same checkpoint location
choices.B: Both streams must have identical schemas
choices.C: A time-range condition (watermark) must be defined on both streams
choices.D: One stream must be converted to a static DataFrame first

questions.shortAnswer: Stream-stream joins require watermarks on both streams to define a time-range condition. This allows Spark to know when old state can be discarded. Checkpoint locations are per-stream. Schemas don't need to match. Both sides remain streaming.

questions.title: Stream-Static Join
questions.question: A streaming pipeline enriches real-time transaction data with customer details from a slowly-changing dimension table. What happens to the static DataFrame in a stream-static join when it's updated?

choices.A: The static side is re-read for each micro-batch, picking up changes
choices.B: The static side is cached at query start and never refreshed
choices.C: The query fails if the static table changes during execution
choices.D: Updates to the static table require restarting the streaming query

questions.shortAnswer: In a stream-static join, the static DataFrame is re-read for each micro-batch. This means updates to the dimension table are automatically picked up without restarting the query. This makes it ideal for slowly-changing dimensions.

questions.title: Stateful Streaming Operations
questions.question: A real-time fraud detection system needs to maintain custom state per user session, tracking cumulative transaction amounts and flagging when thresholds are exceeded within a rolling time window. Which Spark streaming operation provides the most flexibility for this use case?

choices.A: Window aggregation with `groupBy(window(...)).sum()`
choices.B: `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark()` with session tracking
choices.C: `foreachBatch()` with manual state management
choices.D: `flatMapGroupsWithState()` with GroupStateTimeout

questions.shortAnswer: `flatMapGroupsWithState()` provides arbitrary stateful processing with full control over state shape, timeout behavior, and output. Window aggregations are limited to predefined aggregation functions. `foreachBatch()` doesn't maintain state across batches. `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark()` is for dedup only.

questions.title: Advanced Watermarking
questions.question: A streaming aggregation uses a 10-minute watermark. An event arrives with a timestamp 15 minutes behind the current watermark. How does Spark handle this late event?

choices.A: The event is added to the appropriate window and triggers a recomputation
choices.B: The event is silently dropped and not included in any aggregation
choices.C: The event is placed in a special "late data" output stream
choices.D: The query throws a StreamingQueryException for the late data

questions.shortAnswer: Events arriving after the watermark threshold has passed are silently dropped. Spark does not re-open completed windows. There is no "late data" output stream or exception. The watermark defines the boundary for acceptable lateness.

questions.title: Streaming Deduplication
questions.question: An IoT pipeline receives duplicate sensor readings due to at-least-once delivery. Each reading has a `device_id`, `reading_id`, and `event_time`. The pipeline uses a 1-hour watermark. Which approach correctly deduplicates the stream while managing state?

choices.A: `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark("device_id", "reading_id")` with the existing watermark
choices.B: `dropDuplicates("device_id", "reading_id")` without any watermark
choices.C: `MERGE INTO target USING stream ON target.reading_id = stream.reading_id`
choices.D: `groupBy("device_id", "reading_id").count().filter("count = 1")`

questions.shortAnswer: `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark()` uses the existing watermark to bound state size - it only tracks duplicates within the watermark window. `dropDuplicates()` without watermark keeps all keys in state forever, causing unbounded state growth. MERGE is for batch. GroupBy-count doesn't actually deduplicate the output.

questions.title: State Store Configuration
questions.question: A stateful streaming query tracking millions of user sessions is running out of executor memory due to the state store size. Which state store backend should be used for large state volumes?

choices.A: HDFS state store with increased `spark.executor.memory`
choices.B: RocksDB state store backend with `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass`
choices.C: Delta Lake state store for ACID guarantees on state
choices.D: Redis-backed state store for distributed state management

questions.shortAnswer: RocksDB state store uses local disk (SSD) instead of JVM heap memory, allowing much larger state without OOM errors. Configure via `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass=com.databricks.sql.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider`. The default HDFS backend stores state in JVM memory. Delta Lake and Redis state stores are not available in Spark.

questions.title: dbutils.widgets
questions.question: A notebook needs to accept a date parameter that defaults to yesterday's date when not provided. Which code correctly creates this widget?

choices.A: `dbutils.widgets.text("date", str(date.today() - timedelta(days=1)))`
choices.B: `dbutils.widgets.dropdown("date", str(date.today() - timedelta(days=1)), [])`
choices.C: `dbutils.widgets.create("date", default=str(date.today() - timedelta(days=1)))`
choices.D: `dbutils.widgets.parameter("date", str(date.today() - timedelta(days=1)))`

questions.shortAnswer: `dbutils.widgets.text(name, defaultValue)` creates a text input widget with a default value. Option B requires a list of choices. Options C and D are not valid methods.

questions.title: %run Magic Command
questions.question: A main notebook needs to call a utility notebook and use variables defined in it. Which statement is true about `%run`?

choices.A: Variables from the called notebook are not accessible in the calling notebook
choices.B: `%run` executes the notebook asynchronously
choices.C: Variables from the called notebook are available in the calling notebook's scope
choices.D: `%run` can only be used with notebooks in the same folder

questions.shortAnswer: `%run` executes the notebook in the current notebook's context, making all variables and functions available. It runs synchronously and can reference notebooks using relative or absolute paths.

questions.title: Jobs API Run Now
questions.question: A data engineer needs to trigger a job via API with custom parameters. Which API endpoint and method should be used?

choices.A: `POST /api/2.1/jobs/run-now`
choices.B: `GET /api/2.1/jobs/trigger`
choices.C: `POST /api/2.0/jobs/start`
choices.D: `PUT /api/2.1/jobs/execute`

questions.shortAnswer: `POST /api/2.1/jobs/run-now` triggers a job run with optional parameter overrides. This is the current Jobs API version. The other endpoints don't exist.

questions.title: Cluster Types
questions.question: A production ETL job runs daily for 2 hours. Cost optimization is a priority. Which cluster configuration is most cost-effective?

choices.A: All-purpose cluster running 24/7
choices.B: Job cluster created for each run
choices.C: All-purpose cluster with auto-termination
choices.D: Serverless cluster

questions.shortAnswer: Job clusters are created for the job run and terminated after completion. They have lower DBU rates (~60% less than all-purpose) and only incur costs during execution. All-purpose clusters cost more and may have idle time even with auto-termination.

questions.title: Unit Testing with Nutter
questions.question: A team needs to run tests inside Databricks notebooks as part of CI/CD. Which Nutter pattern is correct?

choices.A: `def test_my_function():` followed by assertions
choices.B: `before_`, `run_`, and `assertion_` method prefixes for each test
choices.C: `@test` decorator on test methods
choices.D: `TestCase` class inheritance

questions.shortAnswer: Nutter uses a specific naming convention: `before_<test>` for setup, `run_<test>` for execution, and `assertion_<test>` for verification. This pattern allows tests to run inside Databricks notebooks.

questions.title: Integration Testing Lakeflow Pipelines
questions.question: A team needs to test a Lakeflow pipeline end-to-end as part of CI/CD, validating that expectations pass and output data is correct. What is the recommended approach for integration testing Lakeflow pipelines?

choices.A: Deploy the pipeline to a test target with a test catalog/schema, trigger a full refresh, then validate the output tables and event log
choices.B: Mock the Lakeflow Pipelines framework locally using pytest and validate transformation logic without deploying
choices.C: Run the pipeline in `development` mode which automatically validates all expectations and reports results
choices.D: Use the Lakeflow Pipelines testing API `dlt.test_pipeline()` to run the pipeline in a sandbox environment

questions.shortAnswer: Lakeflow pipelines must run on Databricks infrastructure. Deploy to a test target (using a test catalog/schema for isolation), trigger a full refresh via the API, then query the output tables and event log for expectation results. Local mocking doesn't test Lakeflow Pipelines-specific behavior. Development mode runs the pipeline but doesn't automatically validate outputs. There is no `dlt.test_pipeline()` API.

questions.title: Testing Strategies - Unit vs Integration
questions.question: A data engineer writes a Python function that transforms a DataFrame (adding calculated columns, filtering invalid rows). The function is used inside a Lakeflow pipeline. What is the correct testing strategy for this function?

choices.A: Only test within the Lakeflow pipeline since the function depends on the Lakeflow Pipelines runtime
choices.B: Write integration tests that deploy the full pipeline and verify end-to-end output
choices.C: Use `unittest.mock` to mock the entire SparkSession and DataFrame API
choices.D: Extract the function to a separate module, unit test it with a local SparkSession and sample data, then integration test the full pipeline

questions.shortAnswer: Pure transformation functions should be extracted to testable modules and unit tested locally with a SparkSession (no Lakeflow Pipelines dependency needed). This gives fast feedback. Integration tests run the full pipeline on Databricks for end-to-end validation. Mocking the entire DataFrame API is brittle and doesn't test actual Spark behavior. Testing only in Lakeflow Pipelines is slow and expensive.

questions.title: Streaming Table vs Materialized View
questions.question: A Lakeflow pipeline needs a table that aggregates daily sales totals from a streaming source. Which table type is most appropriate?

choices.A: Streaming table
choices.B: Materialized view
choices.C: Live table
choices.D: Temporary view

questions.shortAnswer: Materialized views are appropriate for aggregations as they fully recompute results. Streaming tables are for append-only incremental processing and don't support aggregations well. "Live table" is deprecated terminology.

questions.title: APPLY CHANGES
questions.question: A CDC pipeline receives insert, update, and delete events. The target table should reflect the current state only. Which APPLY CHANGES configuration is correct?

choices.A: `STORED AS SCD TYPE 1`
choices.B: `STORED AS SCD TYPE 2`
choices.C: `STORED AS SNAPSHOT`
choices.D: `STORED AS CURRENT`

questions.shortAnswer: SCD Type 1 maintains only the current state by overwriting on updates. SCD Type 2 maintains full history with start/end dates. Options C and D are not valid APPLY CHANGES syntax.

questions.title: Lakeflow Pipelines Table Reference
questions.question: A Lakeflow Pipelines SQL query needs to read from another table defined in the same pipeline. How should the source table be referenced?

choices.A: `SELECT * FROM source_table`
choices.B: `SELECT * FROM LIVE.source_table`
choices.C: `SELECT * FROM delta.source_table`
choices.D: `SELECT * FROM dlt.source_table`

questions.shortAnswer: In Lakeflow Pipelines SQL, tables within the pipeline are referenced using the `LIVE.` prefix. This tells Lakeflow Pipelines that the table is defined within the same pipeline and creates the proper dependency.

questions.title: Pipeline Modes
questions.question: A Lakeflow pipeline processes data continuously as it arrives with minimal latency. Which pipeline configuration enables this?

choices.A: `triggered: true`
choices.B: `continuous: true`
choices.C: `development: false`
choices.D: `streaming: true`

questions.shortAnswer: `continuous: true` keeps the pipeline running continuously, processing data as it arrives. Triggered mode (default) processes data in batches when manually started or scheduled. `development` affects cluster size, not processing mode.

questions.title: Full Refresh
questions.question: A schema change requires reprocessing all historical data in a Lakeflow pipeline. How should the pipeline be refreshed?

choices.A: Delete the target tables and restart
choices.B: Use `databricks pipelines start --full-refresh`
choices.C: Set `reset: true` in pipeline configuration
choices.D: Drop and recreate the pipeline

questions.shortAnswer: `--full-refresh` flag clears checkpoints and reprocesses all data from the beginning. This preserves pipeline configuration while resetting state. Manually deleting tables or recreating pipelines is error-prone.

questions.title: Bundle Resource Not Deployed *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team keeps its Declarative Automation Bundle modular: `databricks.yml` at the root, one YAML file per job under `resources/`, and shared code in `src/my_project/`. A developer adds `resources/ingest.job.yml`, runs `databricks bundle deploy -t dev`, and the deployment succeeds, but the new job does not appear in the workspace. What is the most likely fix?

choices.A: Rename the file to `databricks.yml` so the CLI reads it
choices.B: Add the file, or a glob such as `resources/*.yml`, to the top-level `include` mapping in `databricks.yml`
choices.C: Move the job definition into `src/my_project/__init__.py`
choices.D: Run `databricks bundle init default-python` again to regenerate the project

questions.shortAnswer: The resource file must be listed in the top-level `include` mapping.
questions.explanation: A bundle has exactly one `databricks.yml`, and every other configuration file must be listed in `include` (globs relative to the declaring file). A is wrong because a bundle can have only one `databricks.yml`. C is wrong because `src/` holds Python source, not bundle configuration. D regenerates a template and doesn't fix the missing include.

questions.title: Building a Wheel as a Bundle Artifact *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A bundle's `src/my_project/` package must be built into a wheel on every deployment and run by a `python_wheel_task` on serverless compute. Which configuration is correct?

choices.A: An `artifacts` entry with `type: whl` and `build: uv build --wheel`, and a job `environments` spec whose `dependencies` list the built wheel, referenced from the task by `environment_key`
choices.B: An init script that runs `pip install` on the serverless compute at startup
choices.C: A compute-scoped library attached to the serverless compute through the Libraries tab
choices.D: A task-level `libraries` entry only, with no environment, because serverless Python wheel tasks don't need one

questions.shortAnswer: Build the wheel with an `artifacts` entry and install it through a job environment referenced by `environment_key`.
questions.explanation: `artifacts` with `type: whl` builds the package locally before upload, and on serverless, Python wheel and Python script tasks require an environment via `environment_key`. B and C are wrong because serverless doesn't support init scripts or compute-scoped libraries. D is wrong because an environment is required for Python wheel tasks on serverless.

questions.title: Stale Custom Package on Serverless *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A data engineer fixes a bug in an internal Python package, rebuilds the wheel with the same version number `1.4.0`, and redeploys the bundle. The serverless job still behaves as if the old code is installed. What should the engineer do?

choices.A: Add `dbutils.library.restartPython()` at the end of the job's entry point
choices.B: Switch the job to standard performance mode
choices.C: Increase the package version (or set `dynamic_version: true` on the bundle artifact) so the cached environment is not reused
choices.D: Install the package from the DBFS root instead of a Unity Catalog volume

questions.shortAnswer: Change the package version, manually or with `dynamic_version: true`.
questions.explanation: Serverless caches job environments, and Databricks documents that when you change a custom package's implementation you must also update its version number. `dynamic_version: true` patches the wheel version on each deploy. A restarts Python but doesn't change what is installed. B affects startup latency and cost, not dependencies. D is wrong because DBFS-root library storage is deprecated and wouldn't bypass the cache.

questions.title: Private Package Fails Only on Serverless *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A package hosted in an internal Artifactory repository installs correctly on classic clusters, where an init script sets proxy environment variables. When the same notebook runs on serverless compute, installing the package from the Environment side pane fails. Which fix follows Databricks guidance?

choices.A: Set `HTTP_PROXY` with `os.environ` in the first notebook cell before the dependency installs
choices.B: Specify `--index-url` or `--extra-index-url` in the dependency specification, or have an admin configure the repository as a default package repository
choices.C: Attach the init script to the serverless compute through a compute policy
choices.D: Install the package as a Maven coordinate

questions.shortAnswer: Point the dependency at the private index, or configure a workspace default package repository.
questions.explanation: On serverless, dependencies are resolved before any code runs and compute-scoped environment variables aren't supported, so runtime proxy settings have no effect. A fails for that reason. C fails because serverless doesn't support init scripts or compute policies. D is wrong because the package is a Python package and Maven coordinates aren't supported on serverless.

questions.title: Governed Python Function for SQL Warehouses *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team wrote a session-scoped `@udf` that masks email addresses in a notebook. Analysts in several workspaces attached to the same metastore must call it from dashboards on a serverless SQL warehouse, and access must be controlled per group. What should the team do?

choices.A: Register the function with `spark.udf.register` in a shared notebook
choices.B: Convert it to a pandas UDF so it runs faster
choices.C: Create it with `CREATE FUNCTION catalog.schema.mask_email(...) RETURNS STRING LANGUAGE PYTHON AS $$ ... $$` and grant `EXECUTE` to the analyst group
choices.D: Package it in a wheel and install it as a compute-scoped library on the SQL warehouse

questions.shortAnswer: Register it as a Unity Catalog Python UDF and grant `EXECUTE`.
questions.explanation: Unity Catalog functions are persisted, governed with `EXECUTE`, callable from pro and serverless SQL warehouses, and reachable from all workspaces attached to the metastore. A and B create session-scoped functions that exist only in the defining SparkSession. D is wrong because SQL warehouses don't take compute-scoped libraries.

questions.title: Vectorized Governed UDF *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A governed Unity Catalog Python UDF computes a score row by row and is too slow on large tables. The function must stay in Unity Catalog and return exactly one value per input row, and an expensive lookup table should be loaded only once. Which definition fits?

choices.A: `CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS TABLE (...) LANGUAGE PYTHON HANDLER 'Scorer'` with an `eval` method
choices.B: `CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS DOUBLE LANGUAGE PYTHON PARAMETER STYLE PANDAS HANDLER 'handler'`, with the lookup loaded outside the handler that iterates over `pandas.Series` batches
choices.C: A session-scoped `groupBy().applyInPandas()` call in each notebook
choices.D: `CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION ... LANGUAGE SQL` that calls the Python UDF

questions.shortAnswer: Use a Batch Unity Catalog Python UDF with `PARAMETER STYLE PANDAS` and a `HANDLER`.
questions.explanation: Batch Unity Catalog Python UDFs process iterators of `pandas.Series`, must yield the same number of rows as the input, and code outside the handler runs once. A defines a UDTF, which returns tables rather than one value per row. C is session-scoped, not governed, and loads whole groups into memory. D creates a temporary, ungoverned wrapper that still calls the slow row-at-a-time UDF.

questions.title: Cheapest Serverless Nightly Job *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A nightly serverless job has a six-hour SLA and the team wants to minimize DBU consumption. Startup delays of several minutes are acceptable. Which setting should they change?

choices.A: Enable high memory on the job's notebook task
choices.B: Turn off **Performance optimized** so the job uses standard performance mode (`performance_target: STANDARD`)
choices.C: Uncheck **Enable serverless auto-optimization** on every task
choices.D: Attach an instance pool to the serverless job

questions.shortAnswer: Use standard performance mode.
questions.explanation: Standard mode uses less compute and consumes fewer DBUs on the same SKU, with a typical startup of 4 to 6 minutes, which suits batch jobs that tolerate latency. A increases the DBU emission rate. C changes retry behaviour, not cost profile. D is wrong because serverless doesn't support instance pools.

questions.title: Non-Idempotent Serverless Task *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A serverless job task posts invoices to an external billing API and is not idempotent. After a transient failure, invoices were sent twice even though the task's `max_retries` is 0. What should the engineer configure?

choices.A: In the task's retry policy, uncheck **Enable serverless auto-optimization (may include additional retries)** (`disable_auto_optimization: true`)
choices.B: Set `max_retries` to `-1`
choices.C: Switch the task to high memory
choices.D: Pin the serverless environment version

questions.shortAnswer: Disable serverless auto-optimization for the task.
questions.explanation: Serverless auto-optimization is on by default and retries failed tasks; Databricks recommends turning it off for workloads that must run at most once, such as non-idempotent jobs. B retries indefinitely, the opposite of the goal. C and D don't affect retries.

questions.title: Testing a Composed Transformation *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A silver pipeline is written as `df.transform(clean_names).transform(add_net_amount, tax_rate=0.1)`. A `pytest` test compares its output, which contains floating-point amounts and has no defined row order, with an expected DataFrame. Which assertion is most appropriate?

choices.A: `assert actual.collect() == expected.collect()`
choices.B: `assertSchemaEqual(actual, expected)`
choices.C: `assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected, checkRowOrder=True)`
choices.D: `assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected, rtol=1e-5)`

questions.shortAnswer: `assertDataFrameEqual` with a relative tolerance and the default row-order handling.
questions.explanation: `assertDataFrameEqual` compares schema and data, ignores row order by default, and treats floats as equal within `rtol`/`atol`. A depends on row order and exact float equality. B compares only schemas and expects `StructType` arguments, not DataFrames. C would fail because the output isn't sorted.

questions.title: Schema Contract Test *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A downstream team relies on the output columns and types of a `build_gold(df)` function, but the data values change daily. Which test checks only that contract?

choices.A: `assertSchemaEqual(build_gold(df).schema, expected_schema)` where `expected_schema` is a `StructType`
choices.B: `assertDataFrameEqual(build_gold(df), expected_df)`
choices.C: `assert build_gold(df).count() > 0`
choices.D: `assertDataFrameEqual(build_gold(df), [], checkRowOrder=True)`

questions.shortAnswer: Compare the schemas with `assertSchemaEqual`.
questions.explanation: `assertSchemaEqual` compares two `StructType` schemas and raises `[DIFFERENT_SCHEMA]` on mismatch without looking at data. B also compares row values, which change daily. C checks only that rows exist. D compares against an empty list of rows and would fail on any data.

questions.title: Auto Loader Streaming Table *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: JSON files land continuously in a Unity Catalog volume. A data engineer must ingest them into a bronze table in a Lakeflow pipeline so that each file is processed exactly once, new files are picked up incrementally, and schema inference is handled automatically. Which SQL definition meets the requirement?

choices.A: `CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW bronze AS SELECT * FROM read_files('/Volumes/main/landing/orders/', format => 'json')`
choices.B: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files('/Volumes/main/landing/orders/', format => 'json')`
choices.C: A scheduled `COPY INTO bronze` job with `COPY_OPTIONS ('force' = 'true')`
choices.D: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze AS SELECT * FROM read_files('/Volumes/main/landing/orders/', format => 'json')` with `cloudFiles.schemaLocation` set in the pipeline configuration

questions.shortAnswer: A streaming table that reads with `STREAM read_files(...)` uses Auto Loader for incremental, exactly-once file ingestion.
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends streaming tables with Auto Loader for file ingestion, and `read_files` invokes Auto Loader only with the `STREAM` keyword. A is wrong because materialized views should not be defined over Auto Loader ingest; they are recomputed rather than processing each file once. C is wrong because `force = true` reloads every file and creates duplicates. D is wrong because a streaming table's query must be a streaming query, so `STREAM` is required, and pipelines manage the schema location automatically.

questions.title: Auto Loader Schema Evolution Mode *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A bronze streaming table ingests JSON events with Auto Loader in a Lakeflow pipeline. Front-end teams add fields without notice. The team wants the stream never to fail because of schema changes, and wants unexpected fields preserved for later review rather than added as columns. Which `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode` should they set?

choices.A: `addNewColumns`
choices.B: `failOnNewColumns`
choices.C: `rescue`
choices.D: `none`

questions.shortAnswer: `rescue` never evolves the schema, never fails the stream, and records new columns in the rescued data column.
questions.explanation: A is wrong because `addNewColumns` deliberately fails the stream with `UnknownFieldException` after adding the columns and needs a restart. B is wrong because `failOnNewColumns` stops the stream until the schema or the data file is fixed. D is wrong because `none` ignores new columns and does not rescue their data unless a rescued data column is configured.

questions.title: Gold Table Over Updated Silver Data *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A silver orders table is regularly updated with `MERGE` when refunds adjust past orders. A gold table must report revenue per customer that always reflects those adjustments. It is refreshed hourly by a serverless Lakeflow pipeline, and the team wants to avoid recomputing everything when only a few customers change. Which object should the engineer define?

choices.A: A materialized view over the silver table
choices.B: A streaming table that reads the silver table with `skipChangeCommits`
choices.C: A temporary view over the silver table
choices.D: A streaming table that reads the silver table without any options

questions.shortAnswer: A materialized view always matches its query's result over the current source data, and on serverless it refreshes incrementally when the query supports it.
questions.explanation: B is wrong because `skipChangeCommits` ignores update and delete commits, so the refunds would never reach gold. C is wrong because a temporary view is not persisted or published; it is recomputed whenever it is queried and is usable only inside the pipeline. D is wrong because a streaming read fails when its source contains update or delete commits, and a streaming table never revisits rows it already processed.

questions.title: Ingesting from Kafka *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Kafka topic keeps messages for 7 days. The business needs every event kept permanently in a bronze table with latency of a few seconds. Which Lakeflow pipeline design fits?

choices.A: A materialized view that reads the topic with `read_kafka`, refreshed every minute
choices.B: A materialized view over `read_kafka` with `REFRESH POLICY INCREMENTAL STRICT`
choices.C: A temporary view over `read_kafka` queried by downstream tables
choices.D: A streaming table that reads the topic with `STREAM read_kafka(...)` in a continuously running pipeline

questions.shortAnswer: A streaming table processes each Kafka record once and keeps it after the topic's retention expires; continuous execution gives low latency.
questions.explanation: A and B are wrong because the docs warn against defining materialized views on sources that don't retain history, such as Kafka. A recompute would lose events older than the retention period, and MVs are not designed for second-level latency. C is wrong because a view is not persisted, so nothing is kept permanently.

questions.title: Selective SCD Type 2 History *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An AUTO CDC flow maintains an employee dimension. Auditors need a new history row only when `salary` or `department` changes. Frequent changes to `last_login` must update the current row without creating history. Which `dp.create_auto_cdc_flow` arguments meet the requirement?

choices.A: `stored_as_scd_type=1, except_column_list=["last_login"]`
choices.B: `stored_as_scd_type=2, track_history_column_list=["salary", "department"]`
choices.C: `stored_as_scd_type=2, except_column_list=["last_login"]`
choices.D: `stored_as_scd_type=2, apply_as_truncates=expr("operation = 'T'")`

questions.shortAnswer: SCD Type 2 with `track_history_column_list` creates versions only for the listed columns; changes to other columns update the current version in place.
questions.explanation: A is wrong because SCD Type 1 keeps no history at all. C is wrong because `except_column_list` removes `last_login` from the target entirely and every remaining column still creates history. D is wrong because `apply_as_truncates` is supported only for SCD Type 1 and has nothing to do with history tracking.

questions.title: Migrating apply_changes *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A pipeline contains `dlt.apply_changes(target="dim_customer", source="customer_cdc", keys=["id"], sequence_by=col("ts"), stored_as_scd_type=2)`. The engineer is moving it to the current `pyspark.pipelines` API without changing behavior. Which code is correct?

choices.A: `dp.create_streaming_table("dim_customer")` followed by `dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(target="dim_customer", source="customer_cdc", keys=["id"], sequence_by=col("ts"), stored_as_scd_type=2)`
choices.B: An `@dp.materialized_view` named `dim_customer` that runs a `MERGE` against the source
choices.C: `dp.create_auto_cdc_from_snapshot_flow(target="dim_customer", source="customer_cdc", keys=["id"], stored_as_scd_type=2)`
choices.D: A managed table created with `CREATE TABLE dim_customer ... FLOW`, then `dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(...)` with the same arguments

questions.shortAnswer: `create_auto_cdc_flow` replaces `apply_changes` with the same signature, and its target must be a streaming table created first.
questions.explanation: B is wrong because dataset functions must return a DataFrame and must not run writes such as `MERGE`. C is wrong because the snapshot API compares full snapshots and is meant for sources without a change feed; it has no `sequence_by`. D is wrong because managed tables created with `CREATE TABLE ... FLOW` do not support CDC flows and fail with `MANAGED_TABLE_DOES_NOT_SUPPORT_CDC`.

questions.title: When Structured Streaming Fits Better *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team needs a streaming aggregation emitted in **complete** output mode to a custom sink. They also want explicit control over the trigger interval and the checkpoint location, and plan to run it on jobs compute. Which approach fits these operational constraints?

choices.A: A streaming table in a continuous Lakeflow pipeline with its flow set to complete mode
choices.B: A materialized view refreshed every minute by a scheduled pipeline
choices.C: Spark Structured Streaming code scheduled as a Lakeflow Jobs task
choices.D: An AUTO CDC flow with `stored_as_scd_type=1`

questions.shortAnswer: Structured Streaming gives full control over output mode, trigger, sink, and checkpoint location.
questions.explanation: A is wrong because pipelines currently expose only append and update flows, and they manage checkpoints themselves. B is wrong because a materialized view is a batch flow, not a streaming query writing to a custom sink. D is wrong because AUTO CDC applies change events into a streaming table; it is not a complete-mode aggregation to a custom sink.

questions.title: When Declarative Pipelines Fit Better *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A SQL-focused team is building a bronze-silver-gold pipeline. They need automatic dependency ordering, automatic retries of transient failures, data quality rules with pass/fail metrics, lineage, and CDC handling, all with minimal custom code on Databricks. Which approach best fits?

choices.A: Structured Streaming notebooks chained as job tasks, with custom metrics tables
choices.B: Open-source Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines on a self-managed Spark 4.1 cluster
choices.C: Scheduled `COPY INTO` statements in a SQL warehouse
choices.D: Lakeflow Pipelines with streaming tables, materialized views, expectations, and AUTO CDC

questions.shortAnswer: Lakeflow Pipelines infer dependencies, retry failures (task, then flow, then pipeline), and add expectations, AUTO CDC, and a queryable event log on top of SDP.
questions.explanation: A is wrong because the team would have to write and maintain the orchestration, retries, checkpoints, and quality metrics themselves. B is wrong because open-source SDP does not include expectations, AUTO CDC, or the event log; those are Lakeflow additions. C is wrong because `COPY INTO` is batch file loading with no dependency graph, expectations, or CDC handling.

questions.title: Auto Loader Schema Evolution
questions.question: A data engineering team ingests JSON files from cloud storage using Auto Loader. New fields are occasionally added to the source data. Which configuration ensures new columns are automatically added to the target table schema?

choices.A: `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode = "addNewColumns"`
choices.B: `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode = "rescue"`
choices.C: `cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes = "true"`
choices.D: `cloudFiles.mergeSchema = "true"`

questions.shortAnswer: `schemaEvolutionMode = "addNewColumns"` automatically adds new columns to the schema. Option B rescues unexpected data to a separate column. Option C enables type inference but not schema evolution. Option D is not a valid Auto Loader option (that's for Delta writes).

questions.title: OpenSharing
questions.question: A company needs to share data with an external partner who uses Snowflake. Which statement about OpenSharing is correct?

choices.A: The recipient must have a Databricks workspace
choices.B: The recipient can read shared data using any OpenSharing client
choices.C: Data is physically copied to the recipient's storage
choices.D: OpenSharing only works within the same cloud provider

questions.shortAnswer: OpenSharing is an open protocol. Recipients can use any compatible client (Spark, pandas, Power BI, Snowflake, etc.) without needing Databricks. Data is read in place, not copied. It works across cloud providers.

questions.title: Iceberg Readers for a CDC Target *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An AUTO CDC flow in a Lakeflow pipeline maintains an SCD Type 1 streaming table. An external engine using an Iceberg v3 REST catalog client must read this table with read-after-write freshness and **without** a separate data copy. What should the engineer do?

choices.A: Add the table properties `delta.columnMapping.mode = 'name'`, `delta.enableRowTracking = 'true'`, `delta.enableIcebergCompatV3 = 'true'`, `delta.universalFormat.enabledFormats = 'iceberg'`, and `pipelines.externalMetadata.enabled = 'true'` to the streaming table, then run the pipeline
choices.B: Declare the target as `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE ... USING ICEBERG`
choices.C: Set `delta.enableIcebergCompatV2 = 'true'` on the streaming table
choices.D: Enable compatibility mode for the streaming table

questions.shortAnswer: External data access with UniForm Iceberg v3 properties publishes Iceberg metadata for pipeline datasets without copying data.
questions.explanation: B is wrong because for pipeline streaming tables the only `USING` option is `DELTA`. C is wrong because Iceberg reads with IcebergCompatV2 cannot be enabled on streaming tables or materialized views. D is wrong because compatibility mode creates a copy that refreshes on a schedule (hourly by default), which breaks both requirements.

questions.title: Managed Iceberg Gold Object *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: In a Lakeflow pipeline, a gold aggregate computed from a CDC-maintained silver table must be created as an object that external Iceberg readers can read. The workspace has the managed Iceberg materialized view preview enabled. Which definition fits?

choices.A: `STORED AS ICEBERG` added to the AUTO CDC flow that writes the silver table
choices.B: A sink created with `dp.create_sink` using an Iceberg format
choices.C: `CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_summary USING ICEBERG AS SELECT ...`, followed by `REPAIR TABLE gold_summary SYNC METADATA`
choices.D: Legacy change data feed on the silver table so Iceberg readers can consume its changes

questions.shortAnswer: Materialized views accept `USING ICEBERG` (managed Iceberg MVs, Public Preview); after creation you run `REPAIR TABLE ... SYNC METADATA`.
questions.explanation: A is wrong because `STORED AS` only accepts `SCD TYPE 1`, `SCD TYPE 2`, or `BITEMPORAL`. B is wrong because pipeline sinks support Delta, Kafka, Event Hubs, and custom Python data sources, not Iceberg. D is wrong because legacy CDF supports only Delta tables, and change data feed is not part of the Iceberg spec.

questions.title: Kafka Starting Offsets *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A new Structured Streaming query reads an existing Kafka topic with `spark.readStream.format("kafka")` and writes to a Delta table, but the first run ingests none of the messages already in the topic. The engineer then sets `startingOffsets` to `earliest` and restarts the query with the same checkpoint, yet historical messages are still missing. What explains both behaviors?

choices.A: Kafka streaming reads default to `earliest`, so the topic must have been compacted
choices.B: Streaming reads default to `latest`, and `startingOffsets` only applies when a query starts with a new checkpoint
choices.C: `startingOffsets` is ignored unless `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` is also set
choices.D: Delta sinks discard records older than the table's creation time

questions.shortAnswer: Kafka streaming reads default to `startingOffsets = latest`, and the option is honored only for a new query, not one resuming from a checkpoint.
questions.explanation: The Spark options reference states the default is `latest` for streaming (`earliest` for batch) and that resumed queries always use the checkpoint, so a fresh checkpoint location is needed. A is wrong because the streaming default is `latest`. C is wrong because `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` only caps batch size. D is wrong because Delta sinks have no such filter.

questions.title: Binary Files with Auto Loader *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team must incrementally ingest PNG images that land in a Unity Catalog volume alongside other file types, storing each image's path, size, and raw bytes in a Delta table. Which configuration fits?

choices.A: Auto Loader with `cloudFiles.format` set to `binaryFile` and `pathGlobFilter` set to `*.png`
choices.B: Auto Loader with `cloudFiles.format` set to `parquet` and `cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes` set to `true`
choices.C: `spark.readStream.format("delta")` pointed at the volume path
choices.D: `COPY INTO` with `FILEFORMAT = ICEBERG`

questions.shortAnswer: Auto Loader supports `binaryFile`, which returns `path`, `modificationTime`, `length`, and `content` per file, and `pathGlobFilter` selects the suffix.
questions.explanation: The Auto Loader patterns docs show exactly this `binaryFile` + `pathGlobFilter` combination because the path is only a prefix filter. B is wrong because images are not Parquet. C is wrong because the volume contains raw files, not a Delta table. D is wrong because Iceberg is a table format, not a file format for `COPY INTO`.

questions.title: Choosing a CDC Ingestion Approach *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An operational SQL Server database must be continuously replicated into Unity Catalog, including updates and deletes, with minimal custom code and full row history kept for a customer dimension table. Which approach meets the requirement?

choices.A: A nightly JDBC full-table read that overwrites the target table
choices.B: A Lakehouse Federation foreign catalog queried by a materialized view
choices.C: A Lakeflow Connect SQL Server connector with CDC enabled on the source table and `scd_type` set to `SCD_TYPE_2`
choices.D: A Lakeflow Connect SQL Server connector using change tracking with `scd_type` set to `SCD_TYPE_2`

questions.shortAnswer: The managed SQL Server connector with source CDC enabled and `SCD_TYPE_2` replicates changes continuously and keeps history.
questions.explanation: Lakeflow Connect docs note that SCD type 2 requires CDC on the source and that change tracking does not support `SCD_TYPE_2`, which rules out D. A misses changes between runs and keeps no history. B queries the source live without replicating changes or history.

questions.title: Ingestion Gateway Behavior *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team uses a gateway-based Lakeflow Connect PostgreSQL pipeline. To save money, an engineer stops the ingestion gateway each night and restarts it in the morning, while the ingestion pipeline runs hourly on serverless. What is the main risk?

choices.A: The serverless ingestion pipeline cannot start while the gateway is stopped
choices.B: Changes can be lost to source log retention, forcing a full refresh of affected tables
choices.C: The staging volume is deleted whenever the gateway stops
choices.D: The destination streaming tables lose their change data feed

questions.shortAnswer: The gateway must run continuously to capture changes before the source truncates its change logs; stopping it can drop changes and require full refreshes.
questions.explanation: The docs warn not to stop the gateway, which runs on classic compute as a continuous pipeline. A is wrong because the ingestion pipeline can run on its own schedule from staging data. C is wrong because staged data is purged after 30 days, not on stop. D is wrong because CDF is enabled on all target tables regardless.

questions.title: D2D Recipient Setup *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A provider wants to share curated tables, a Unity Catalog volume, and a notebook with a partner whose Databricks workspace is enabled for Unity Catalog in another account, without managing any tokens. What should the provider do?

choices.A: Run `CREATE RECIPIENT partner USING ID '<cloud>:<region>:<uuid>'` with the partner's sharing identifier, then `GRANT SELECT ON SHARE s TO RECIPIENT partner`
choices.B: Run `CREATE RECIPIENT partner` and send the activation link for the credential file
choices.C: Grant `USE CATALOG` on the source catalog directly to the partner's account users
choices.D: Create an OIDC federation recipient and share the volume through an Iceberg REST client

questions.shortAnswer: A Databricks-to-Databricks recipient identified by the partner metastore's sharing identifier needs no tokens and supports volumes and notebooks.
questions.explanation: The OpenSharing docs say D2D supports notebook, volume, and model sharing, which Databricks-to-Open does not. B creates a token-based Databricks-to-Open recipient that cannot receive volumes or notebooks. C does not work across metastores in different accounts. D is a Databricks-to-Open method and still cannot carry volumes.

questions.title: Sharing a Table Subset *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A provider has one share for many regional partners and wants each recipient to see only rows for its own country from a partitioned table, without creating a separate share per partner. Which approach works?

choices.A: `ALTER SHARE s ADD TABLE t WITH PARTITION (country = 'US')` for each partner
choices.B: Set a `country` recipient property and add the table with `PARTITION (country = CURRENT_RECIPIENT().country)`
choices.C: Add row filters to the source table and share it directly
choices.D: Share the table `WITHOUT HISTORY` so recipients only see current rows

questions.shortAnswer: Recipient properties referenced with `CURRENT_RECIPIENT()` in the partition spec let one share filter partitions per recipient.
questions.explanation: The `ALTER SHARE` reference documents `PARTITION (column = CURRENT_RECIPIENT().<property-key>)`. A uses invalid `WITH PARTITION` syntax and still needs per-partner shares. C fails because tables with row filters or column masks cannot be shared. D controls history, not row visibility.

questions.title: Clean Room vs Share *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An advertiser and a publisher, both on Databricks with Unity Catalog, want to compute audience overlap on hashed emails. Neither may see the other's rows, and both want to review any code before it touches their data. What should they use?

choices.A: A Databricks-to-Databricks OpenSharing share in each direction
choices.B: A Databricks clean room with notebooks approved by the other collaborator and run by a designated runner
choices.C: Lakehouse Federation from each workspace into the other
choices.D: A Databricks Marketplace private exchange

questions.shortAnswer: Clean Rooms share data only into a central clean room, expose only metadata to collaborators, and run only notebooks approved by every other collaborator.
questions.explanation: The Clean Rooms docs describe this no-trust model. A gives each recipient read access to the other's rows. C also exposes the data for direct querying. D distributes data products and gives no code approval or row protection.

questions.title: Clean Room Output *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: In an approval-based clean room, a notebook run writes results with `cr_output_catalog` and `cr_output_schema`. The other collaborator complains they cannot read the results. What explains this, and what fixes it for future runs?

choices.A: Output tables are readable only by the runner by default; create a new clean room with shared output enabled and write to `cr_shared_output_schema`
choices.B: Output tables expire after one hour; rerun the notebook more often
choices.C: The collaborator lacks `MODIFY CLEAN ROOM`; grant it on the clean room
choices.D: Output tables are views; convert them to tables with `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT`

questions.shortAnswer: By default only the runner can read output tables; shared output, set when the clean room is created, lets all collaborators read tables in `cr_shared_output_schema`.
questions.explanation: The output-tables docs state shared output can't be changed after creation, so a new clean room is required. B is wrong because outputs are kept 30 days. C is wrong because `MODIFY CLEAN ROOM` manages assets, not output access. D is wrong because only tables are supported as output.

questions.title: Federation Privileges *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An admin created a Unity Catalog connection to a PostgreSQL database with credentials stored through `secret()`. A data engineer must now create a foreign catalog from it, and analysts must only query one table. Which grants are needed?

choices.A: Engineer: `USE CONNECTION` on the connection; analysts: the PostgreSQL password
choices.B: Engineer: `CREATE CATALOG` on the metastore and `CREATE FOREIGN CATALOG` on the connection; analysts: `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, and `SELECT` on the foreign objects
choices.C: Engineer: `CREATE CONNECTION` on the metastore; analysts: `USE CONNECTION` on the connection
choices.D: Engineer: `ALL PRIVILEGES` on the metastore; analysts: `BROWSE` on the connection

questions.shortAnswer: Creating a foreign catalog requires `CREATE CATALOG` on the metastore plus `CREATE FOREIGN CATALOG` on the connection, and readers need normal UC data privileges.
questions.explanation: Query federation docs list these requirements, and credentials come from the connection so readers never need them. A exposes credentials and `USE CONNECTION` doesn't allow catalog creation. C's `CREATE CONNECTION` creates connections, not catalogs, and `USE CONNECTION` doesn't grant table reads. D over-grants and `BROWSE` doesn't allow querying.

questions.title: Query vs Catalog Federation *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A company is migrating tables registered in AWS Glue to Unity Catalog incrementally. During the migration, users must query Glue tables through Unity Catalog with UC access control, running only on Databricks compute and reading files directly from S3. Which approach fits?

choices.A: Query federation over JDBC to Glue
choices.B: Catalog federation with a Glue connection, external locations, and a foreign catalog with authorized paths
choices.C: A Lakeflow Connect database connector for Glue
choices.D: An OpenSharing share from Glue

questions.shortAnswer: Catalog federation reads foreign tables directly from object storage on Databricks compute and is documented for Glue-based incremental migrations.
questions.explanation: Setup needs a connection, external locations for the table paths, and a foreign catalog with authorized paths. A describes query federation, which pushes SQL to a database engine and doesn't apply to Glue. C is wrong because Lakeflow Connect database connectors read relational change logs. D is wrong because Glue is not an OpenSharing provider.

questions.title: MERGE Operation
questions.question: A data engineer needs to update existing records and insert new ones from a source table into a target Delta table. Which MERGE clause handles records that exist in the source but not in the target?

choices.A: `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE`
choices.B: `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT`
choices.C: `WHEN MATCHED THEN INSERT`
choices.D: `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE`

questions.shortAnswer: `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` handles source records that don't have a matching key in the target. `WHEN MATCHED` handles existing records. Option C is invalid syntax. Option D handles records in target not in source.

questions.title: Delta Lake Time Travel
questions.question: A user accidentally deleted important records 3 days ago. The table has default retention settings. Which command restores the data?

choices.A: `RESTORE TABLE orders TO VERSION AS OF 100`
choices.B: `SELECT * FROM orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-01-12'`
choices.C: `ROLLBACK TABLE orders TO 3 DAYS AGO`
choices.D: Both A and B can be used to access historical data

questions.shortAnswer: Both version-based (`VERSION AS OF`) and timestamp-based (`TIMESTAMP AS OF`) time travel work. RESTORE actually reverts the table, while SELECT reads historical data. Default retention is 7 days, so 3-day-old data is available.

questions.title: Expectations
questions.question: A Lakeflow pipeline requires that all records have a non-null customer_id. Invalid records should be removed but not fail the pipeline. Which expectation syntax achieves this?

choices.A: `CONSTRAINT valid_id EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL)`
choices.B: `CONSTRAINT valid_id EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`
choices.C: `CONSTRAINT valid_id EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE`
choices.D: `@dlt.expect_all("valid_id", "customer_id IS NOT NULL")`

questions.shortAnswer: `ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` removes invalid records without failing the pipeline. Option A only logs warnings but keeps invalid rows. Option C fails the entire pipeline. Option D has incorrect syntax.

questions.title: Quarantining Bad Records *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: Records that fail two validation rules must not reach the silver path but must be kept for review. The team wants per-rule pass/fail metrics, and the pipeline must keep running. Which implementation fits?

choices.A: `@dp.expect_all_or_drop(rules)` on the silver table only
choices.B: A private table with `@dp.expect_all(rules)` that adds `is_quarantined = NOT(<all rules>)`, plus valid and invalid views that filter on that flag
choices.C: `@dp.expect_all_or_fail(rules)` on the silver table
choices.D: `CONSTRAINT valid EXPECT (...) ON VIOLATION QUARANTINE ROW`

questions.shortAnswer: The documented quarantine pattern uses warn-level expectations for metrics and a computed flag to split valid and invalid rows without losing any.
questions.explanation: A is wrong because dropped rows are only counted, not kept for review. C is wrong because a fail expectation stops the flow's update instead of routing the rows. D is wrong because the only `ON VIOLATION` actions are `DROP ROW` and `FAIL UPDATE`.

questions.title: Fail Expectation Behavior *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A **triggered** Lakeflow pipeline has a materialized view `gold_balances` with `@dp.expect_or_fail("non_negative", "balance >= 0")`. An independent streaming table in the same pipeline ingests clickstream data. During an update, one balance is negative. What happens?

choices.A: The violating row is dropped and counted as a dropped record in the event log
choices.B: Every flow in the pipeline, including the clickstream table, fails and rolls back
choices.C: The row is written to `gold_balances` and a warning metric is recorded
choices.D: The `gold_balances` flow fails and its update is rolled back, while the independent clickstream flow continues to update

questions.shortAnswer: In a triggered pipeline, a fail expectation fails and atomically rolls back only that flow's update; other parallel flows are not failed.
questions.explanation: A describes `expect_or_drop`. B is wrong because only in continuous mode does a failure also stop dependent flows, and an unrelated flow is not affected in triggered mode. C describes the default warn action. Note also that no expectation metrics are recorded for an update that fails.

questions.title: Tolerant JSON Parsing into VARIANT *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Bronze table receives webhook payloads as JSON strings in a column named `raw`. About 0.1 % of payloads are malformed. The Silver job must convert every payload to a `VARIANT` column without failing the whole batch, and it must keep a `NULL` for unparseable payloads so they can be quarantined later. Which expression should the engineer use?

choices.A: `parse_json(raw)`
choices.B: `try_parse_json(raw)`
choices.C: `to_json(raw)`
choices.D: `variant_get(raw, '$', 'variant')`

questions.shortAnswer: `try_parse_json(raw)` returns a `VARIANT` for valid JSON and `NULL` for malformed input, so the batch keeps running.
questions.explanation: `try_parse_json` is the error-tolerant version of `parse_json`, and its `NULL` result can be routed to a quarantine table. `parse_json` (A) raises `MALFORMED_RECORD_IN_PARSING` on invalid JSON and would fail the batch. `to_json` (C) goes the other way, turning a `STRUCT` or `VARIANT` into a JSON string. `variant_get` (D) extracts typed values from an existing `VARIANT` expression and can't parse a string.

questions.title: Clustering on a Field Inside VARIANT *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Silver table stores clickstream events in a single `payload VARIANT` column. Most queries filter on `payload:customer_id` and `payload:event_ts`, and scans are slow. The team wants file-level data skipping on those two attributes while keeping the rest of the payload flexible. Which design should the engineer choose?

choices.A: Run `ALTER TABLE events CLUSTER BY (payload)` and then `OPTIMIZE`
choices.B: Recreate the table with `PARTITIONED BY (payload:customer_id)`
choices.C: Extract `payload:customer_id::BIGINT` and `payload:event_ts::TIMESTAMP` into typed top-level columns, keep `payload` as `VARIANT`, and cluster on the new columns
choices.D: Run `OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (payload)`

questions.shortAnswer: Promote the frequently filtered fields to typed columns, keep the rest as `VARIANT`, and liquid-cluster on the typed columns.
questions.explanation: `VARIANT` columns can't be partition, clustering, or Z-order keys, and they don't collect min/max statistics. Databricks recommends extracting frequently queried fields into non-variant columns to speed up queries and improve layout. Options A, B, and D all try to use the `VARIANT` column, or an expression on it, as a layout key, which isn't supported. Partition columns must also be top-level columns rather than expressions.

questions.title: Keeping Large ai_query Batches Running *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A nightly job enriches 40 million product reviews with `ai_query('system.ai.meta-llama-3-3-70b-instruct', prompt || review_text)`. A handful of rows hit model endpoint errors each night, the whole query fails, and all completed inferences are lost. What should the engineer change to keep the successful results and still identify the failed rows?

choices.A: Add `failOnError => false` and write rows where `result.errorMessage IS NOT NULL` to a retry table
choices.B: Split the input into 1,000-row batches and run them in a Python loop
choices.C: Wrap the call in `try_cast(... AS STRING)`
choices.D: Add `modelParameters => named_struct('temperature', 0.0)`

questions.shortAnswer: With `failOnError => false`, `ai_query` returns a `STRUCT` with `response` and `errorMessage`, so the job completes and failed rows can be found.
questions.explanation: The docs recommend `failOnError => false` for large workloads. A row with a model endpoint error gets a `NULL` `response` and a populated `errorMessage`, and successful rows are kept. Manual micro-batching (B) is discouraged because AI Functions already handle parallelization, retries, and scaling, and smaller batches can lower throughput. `try_cast` (C) doesn't intercept inference errors. Model parameters (D) change generation behavior, not error handling. `temperature` already defaults to 0.0 in `ai_query`.

questions.title: Ticket Routing with Minimal Prompt Engineering *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Lakeflow pipeline must route incoming support tickets to one of five known queues (billing, defect, account, feature request, other). The team has no custom model, wants no prompt engineering, and needs the output to be exactly one of the five label names so downstream routing logic doesn't break. Which approach fits best?

choices.A: `ai_summarize(body, 5)` followed by `regexp_extract` to find a queue name
choices.B: `ai_gen('Which queue should this ticket go to? ' || body)`
choices.C: `ai_query` against a chat model with a free-form prompt and no `responseFormat`
choices.D: `ai_classify(body, '["billing", "defect", "account", "feature_request", "other"]', map('version', '2.1'))`

questions.shortAnswer: `ai_classify` is the task-specific function for classifying text into labels you provide, and it returns label names that exactly match the `labels` argument.
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends starting with a task-specific AI Function when one matches the task. `ai_classify` needs no prompt, accepts label descriptions and instructions, and in version 2.x returns a `VARIANT` whose `response[0].value` is one of the supplied labels. Option A is a fragile workaround on a summary. `ai_gen` (B) and an unconstrained `ai_query` (C) produce free text that might not match a queue name. `ai_query` is meant for cases that need a specific model, prompt, or output schema.

questions.title: System Tables
questions.question: A data engineer needs to track compute costs by team over the past month. Which system table provides this information?

choices.A: `system.access.audit`
choices.B: `system.billing.usage`
choices.C: `system.compute.clusters`
choices.D: `system.query.history`

questions.shortAnswer: `system.billing.usage` contains cost and usage data including DBUs consumed. `audit` tracks access events. `clusters` contains cluster metadata. `query.history` tracks SQL queries, not costs.

questions.title: Lakeflow Pipelines Event Log
questions.question: A Lakeflow pipeline ran with data quality issues. The team needs to find how many records failed expectations. How can this information be retrieved?

choices.A: Query the Delta table directly
choices.B: Check the Spark UI
choices.C: Query the pipeline's event log
choices.D: Review the cluster logs

questions.shortAnswer: The Lakeflow Pipelines event log contains expectation metrics including passed/failed record counts. Query it using `event_log(TABLE(pipeline))` or access via the system tables. The event log provides detailed pipeline observability.

questions.title: Attribute DBU Spend to Jobs *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A data engineer must report last month's list cost per job. They join `system.billing.usage` to `system.billing.list_prices` only on `sku_name` and the totals come out several times higher than the invoice. What change fixes the join?

choices.A: Filter `system.billing.usage` to `record_type = 'ORIGINAL'` only
choices.B: Also join on `cloud` and require `usage_start_time` to fall between `price_start_time` and `price_end_time` (or `price_end_time IS NULL`)
choices.C: Replace `pricing.default` with `usage_quantity` from `list_prices`
choices.D: Join to `system.compute.clusters` on `sku_name` instead

questions.shortAnswer: Join on `cloud`, `sku_name`, and the price validity window.
questions.explanation: `list_prices` stores one row per price change, so joining on `sku_name` alone multiplies each usage row by every historical price. The docs join on `cloud`, `sku_name`, and `usage_start_time >= price_start_time AND (usage_end_time <= price_end_time OR price_end_time IS NULL)`, then multiply by `pricing.default`. Filtering to ORIGINAL rows (A) would drop corrections that should be summed. `list_prices` has no `usage_quantity` (C). `compute.clusters` has no prices and no `sku_name` (D).

questions.title: Missing Job Cost in Billing *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team notices that several scheduled jobs never appear when they group `system.billing.usage` by `usage_metadata.job_id`, even though `system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline` shows the jobs ran successfully every day. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.A: The jobs ran on all-purpose compute, where `usage_metadata.job_id` is not populated
choices.B: Billing records for jobs are only written after 365 days
choices.C: `usage_metadata.job_id` is only populated for jobs triggered by the REST API
choices.D: The jobs ran in a different region, so `system.billing.usage` cannot see them

questions.shortAnswer: `job_id` is populated only for jobs on job compute or serverless compute.
questions.explanation: The billable usage reference states that `usage_metadata.job_id` and `job_run_id` are populated for serverless jobs and jobs on job compute, but not for jobs run on all-purpose compute. That usage can only be approximated through `cluster_id`. Billing arrives within hours, not after 365 days (B). The trigger type doesn't matter (C). `system.billing.usage` is a global table that covers every region (D).

questions.title: Monitor Failed Pipeline Events from a Script *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A data engineer writes a Python CI check that must fail when a Lakeflow pipeline logged any ERROR events. They use the Databricks SDK for Python with `w = WorkspaceClient()`. Which call returns those events?

choices.A: `w.jobs.get_run_output(run_id=pipeline_id)`
choices.B: `w.pipelines.list_updates(pipeline_id=pid, filter="level='ERROR'")`
choices.C: `w.pipelines.list_pipeline_events(pipeline_id=pid, filter="level='ERROR'")`
choices.D: `w.pipelines.get(pipeline_id=pid).events`

questions.shortAnswer: Use `list_pipeline_events` with `filter="level='ERROR'"`.
questions.explanation: `list_pipeline_events` (REST `GET /api/2.0/pipelines/{pipeline_id}/events`, CLI `databricks pipelines list-pipeline-events`) supports SQL-like filters such as `level='ERROR'` and `timestamp > '...'`. `list_updates` lists updates and takes no level filter (B). `get_run_output` is for job task runs (A). `GetPipelineResponse` has `state`, `health`, and `latest_updates`, but no `events` attribute (D).

questions.title: Why Did a Task Fail via the Jobs API *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A multitask job run failed. An engineer calls the Jobs API `runs/get-output` with the job run's `run_id` and gets an error instead of the task's stack trace. What should they do?

choices.A: Use Jobs API 2.0, because 2.2 removed run output
choices.B: Call `runs/get` for the job run, then call `runs/get-output` with the failed task's `run_id` from `tasks[]`
choices.C: Call `runs/list` with `expand_tasks=true`, which returns `error_trace`
choices.D: Read `state.result_state` from `runs/get`, which contains the stack trace

questions.shortAnswer: Pass the task run ID from `runs/get` to `runs/get-output`.
questions.explanation: `runs/get-output` (SDK `get_run_output`) returns the output, `error`, and `error_trace` of a single task run, so you first read `tasks[].run_id` from `runs/get`. Jobs API 2.2 still provides run output (A). `runs/list` returns run metadata, not error traces (C). `state` is deprecated, and its `result_state` is only an enum (D).

questions.title: Branch a Job on an Alert *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A job refreshes a silver table and then must run a quarantine notebook only when a Databricks SQL alert on null rates is TRIGGERED, and otherwise publish to gold. The engineer adds a SQL alert task, but the quarantine step never runs, even when the alert triggers, because the alert task always shows Succeeded. What should they add?

choices.A: Set `run_if: AT_LEAST_ONE_FAILED` on the quarantine task
choices.B: An If/else condition task comparing `{{tasks.<alert_task>.output.alert_state}}` to `TRIGGERED`, with quarantine depending on the true outcome and publish on the false outcome
choices.C: A schedule on the underlying alert so it runs before the job
choices.D: Increase the alert task's retries so it fails when triggered

questions.shortAnswer: Add an If/else condition task on `output.alert_state`.
questions.explanation: A SQL alert task reports Succeeded whenever evaluation completes, whether or not the alert triggered. It fails only on evaluation errors. The dynamic value `{{tasks.<task>.output.alert_state}}` (UNKNOWN, OK, or TRIGGERED) feeds an If/else task whose dependents use the true and false outcomes. `AT_LEAST_ONE_FAILED` never fires because the task succeeds (A). The alert's own schedule is independent of the job (C). Retries don't change a successful evaluation (D).

questions.title: Schema-Wide Freshness Alerts *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A platform team wants Slack notifications whenever any table in the `main.sales` schema becomes stale or receives far fewer rows than usual, without writing or maintaining SQL for each table. Which approach fits best?

choices.A: Create one Databricks SQL alert per table on `DESCRIBE HISTORY`
choices.B: Enable anomaly detection on the schema and create a Data Quality Monitoring alert rule scoped to `main.sales` with a Slack notification destination
choices.C: Configure a budget in the account console with the schema as a tag filter
choices.D: Add a duration warning health rule to every job that writes the schema

questions.shortAnswer: Use anomaly detection with a Data Quality Monitoring alert rule.
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection checks freshness and completeness for every table in a schema. Alert rules created in the Data Quality Monitoring UI are scoped to a catalog or schema and notify users or destinations such as Slack, with no SQL to write. A SQL alert per table (A) means manual work for each table. Budgets track spend, not data quality (C). Job duration warnings track run time, not table freshness (D).

questions.title: Interpret Job Run Status *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: In the Lakeflow Jobs UI, a multitask job run shows Succeeded with failures. What does this mean?

choices.A: All tasks succeeded after at least one retry
choices.B: Some tasks failed, but all leaf tasks succeeded
choices.C: The run exceeded its duration warning threshold
choices.D: The run was skipped because of max concurrent runs

questions.shortAnswer: Some tasks failed, but every leaf task succeeded.
questions.explanation: The run outcome is determined by the leaf tasks, the tasks with no downstream dependencies. Succeeded with failures means some tasks failed but all leaf tasks succeeded, and notifications treat it as a success. Retries that eventually succeed show as Succeeded (A). Exceeding a duration threshold triggers a warning, not a status (C). A run blocked by concurrency limits is Skipped (D).

questions.title: Find the Slow Phase of a Job Run *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A scheduled job on classic compute has recently started finishing 15 minutes later than usual, even though its code and data volume are unchanged. In the Jobs UI, where can an engineer quickly see whether the extra time is spent queueing, waiting for compute, installing libraries, or running?

choices.A: The run breakdown shown when hovering the run's Duration on the job run details page
choices.B: The Spark UI event timeline of the driver
choices.C: The Top 5 error types table on the Runs tab
choices.D: The `system.billing.usage` table filtered by `job_run_id`

questions.shortAnswer: Hover the run's Duration to see the run breakdown by phase.
questions.explanation: The job run details page breaks Duration into Queued, Waiting for resources, Library installation, and Running, for both job runs and task runs. The Spark UI (B) only covers execution inside Spark. The Top 5 error types table (C) summarizes failures. Billing (D) shows DBUs, not a timing breakdown.

questions.title: Change Data Feed
questions.question: A data engineer needs to track all changes (inserts, updates, deletes) to a Delta table for downstream CDC processing. Which statement correctly enables this capability?

choices.A: `ALTER TABLE orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableChangeDataCapture' = true)`
choices.B: `ALTER TABLE orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableChangeDataFeed' = true)`
choices.C: `ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE CHANGE TRACKING`
choices.D: `CREATE TABLE orders WITH (CDC = ENABLED)`

questions.shortAnswer: `delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true` enables Change Data Feed (CDF) on a Delta table. This allows reading changes using `table_changes()` function or `readChangeData` option. The other options use incorrect syntax.

questions.title: Back-Pressure and Rate Limiting
questions.question: A streaming query reads from Kafka and the processing time per micro-batch is consistently exceeding the trigger interval, causing increasing latency. Which configuration limits the amount of data processed per micro-batch?

choices.A: `trigger(processingTime="10 seconds")` to increase batch frequency
choices.B: `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.maintenanceInterval` to reduce state overhead
choices.C: `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to increase parallelism
choices.D: `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` to limit records consumed from Kafka per batch

questions.shortAnswer: `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` controls the maximum number of offsets (records) read from Kafka per trigger, providing back-pressure control. Changing the trigger interval doesn't reduce per-batch data. State maintenance affects state cleanup, not ingestion. Shuffle partitions affect parallelism, not input volume.

questions.title: Liquid Clustering vs Z-ORDER
questions.question: A table is frequently filtered by `customer_id` and `order_date`. The team wants automatic optimization. Which approach provides automatic maintenance?

choices.A: `OPTIMIZE table ZORDER BY (customer_id, order_date)` scheduled daily
choices.B: `ALTER TABLE table CLUSTER BY (customer_id, order_date)`
choices.C: `CREATE TABLE table PARTITIONED BY (customer_id, order_date)`
choices.D: Both A and B provide automatic maintenance

questions.shortAnswer: Liquid Clustering (`CLUSTER BY`) provides automatic, incremental clustering without manual OPTIMIZE commands. Z-ORDER requires scheduled OPTIMIZE runs. Partitioning is for low-cardinality columns and doesn't cluster data within partitions.

questions.title: Query Profiler
questions.question: A SQL query is running slowly. The data engineer wants to see if partition pruning is working. What should they look for in EXPLAIN output?

choices.A: `PartitionFilters` showing filter conditions
choices.B: `DataFilters` showing filter conditions
choices.C: `PushedFilters` showing filter conditions
choices.D: All of the above indicate different types of filtering

questions.shortAnswer: `PartitionFilters` shows partition pruning (best). `DataFilters` shows filters applied after scan. `PushedFilters` shows filters pushed to the file format. Ideally, filters should appear in PartitionFilters for best performance.

questions.title: Identifying Data Skew
questions.question: A job has 99 tasks completing in 1 minute but one task takes 30 minutes. What is the most likely cause?

choices.A: Insufficient cluster memory
choices.B: Data skew in partition keys
choices.C: Network timeout
choices.D: Corrupt data file

questions.shortAnswer: One task taking much longer than others typically indicates data skew - one partition has significantly more data. Solutions include salting keys, using AQE skew handling, or repartitioning data more evenly.

questions.title: OPTIMIZE and ZORDER
questions.question: A table frequently filters on `region` and `date` columns. Small files are causing performance issues. Which command best optimizes query performance?

choices.A: `OPTIMIZE table_name`
choices.B: `OPTIMIZE table_name ZORDER BY (region)`
choices.C: `OPTIMIZE table_name ZORDER BY (region, date)`
choices.D: `VACUUM table_name`

questions.shortAnswer: ZORDER on both frequently filtered columns provides the best data skipping. Option A compacts files but doesn't optimize data layout. Option B only optimizes for one column. VACUUM removes old files but doesn't improve layout.

questions.title: Shuffle Partitions
questions.question: A Spark job processing 10GB of data is running slowly with default settings. What is the default value of `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` and how should it be adjusted?

choices.A: 100; increase for large data
choices.B: 200; decrease for small data
choices.C: 200; increase for large data
choices.D: 500; keep default for all data

questions.shortAnswer: Default is 200. For 10GB (relatively small), reducing partitions can improve performance by reducing overhead. Rule of thumb: target ~128MB per partition. 10GB / 128MB = 80 partitions.

questions.title: Broadcast Join
questions.question: A large fact table (100GB) is joined with a small dimension table (50MB). How can the join be optimized?

choices.A: Increase shuffle partitions
choices.B: Use a broadcast hint on the large table
choices.C: Use a broadcast hint on the small table
choices.D: Partition both tables by the join key

questions.shortAnswer: Broadcasting the small table avoids shuffling the large table. The small table is sent to all executors for a local join. Default broadcast threshold is 10MB, so a hint may be needed for 50MB: `/*+ BROADCAST(small_table) */`.

questions.title: AQE (Adaptive Query Execution)
questions.question: A query has skewed data causing one task to run much longer than others. Which AQE feature helps with this?

choices.A: Coalesce partitions
choices.B: Skew join optimization
choices.C: Dynamic broadcast join
choices.D: Local shuffle reader
