questions.shortAnswer: AQE's skew join optimization automatically detects and splits skewed partitions to distribute work more evenly. Coalesce combines small partitions. Dynamic broadcast switches join strategies. Local shuffle reader reduces I/O.

questions.title: File Size Optimization
questions.question: A streaming job creates many small files, degrading query performance. Which configuration helps?

choices.A: `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 1`
choices.B: `delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite = true`
choices.C: `spark.databricks.delta.vacuum.enabled = true`
choices.D: `delta.checkpoint.writeStatsAsJson = false`

questions.shortAnswer: `optimizeWrite` bins data during writes to create better-sized files. This is especially helpful for streaming which naturally creates small files. Option A would create single-file outputs (bad for parallelism). Vacuum removes old files but doesn't compact.

questions.title: Cost Optimization
questions.question: A daily ETL job runs for 3 hours. The team wants to reduce costs. Which change provides the biggest cost savings?

choices.A: Switch from all-purpose to job cluster
choices.B: Increase cluster size to finish faster
choices.C: Run during business hours
choices.D: Disable auto-scaling

questions.shortAnswer: Job clusters have ~60% lower DBU rates than all-purpose clusters. They're created for the job and terminated after, eliminating idle time costs. Larger clusters may cost more overall. Auto-scaling typically helps with costs.

questions.title: EXPLAIN Plan Analysis
questions.question: A data engineer runs `EXPLAIN EXTENDED` on a slow query and sees `SortMergeJoin` in the physical plan where one table is only 5MB. What does this indicate and how should it be fixed?

choices.A: The join is optimal; SortMergeJoin is always the fastest strategy
choices.B: Add a Z-ORDER on the join key to improve data locality
choices.C: The broadcast threshold is too low; increase `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` or add a broadcast hint
choices.D: The query needs more shuffle partitions to distribute the sort

questions.shortAnswer: A 5MB table should be broadcast-joined (avoiding shuffle), not sort-merge-joined. The default threshold is 10MB, but if statistics are inaccurate, Spark may choose SortMergeJoin. Increasing the threshold or using `/*+ BROADCAST(t) */` forces the more efficient BroadcastHashJoin.

questions.title: Photon Engine
questions.question: A team enables Photon on their cluster expecting all queries to run faster. Some queries show improvement while others show no change. Which workload type benefits MOST from Photon acceleration?

choices.A: Machine learning model training with MLlib
choices.B: Scan-heavy queries with aggregations and joins on large Delta tables
choices.C: Python UDF-heavy transformations
choices.D: Streaming micro-batches with very small data volumes

questions.shortAnswer: Photon is a C++ vectorized execution engine optimized for scan-heavy SQL/DataFrame operations including aggregations, joins, and filters. It doesn't accelerate Python UDFs (which run in Python), MLlib (which uses different execution paths), or very small data volumes (where overhead exceeds benefit).

questions.title: Memory and Spill Diagnostics
questions.question: A Spark job shows "spill to disk" warnings in the Spark UI. The job completes but is much slower than expected. What is the primary cause of disk spill and the best remediation?

choices.A: Disk spill is caused by too many tasks; reduce `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`
choices.B: Disk spill is caused by insufficient CPU cores; increase cluster size
choices.C: Disk spill indicates corrupted data blocks; run OPTIMIZE on source tables
choices.D: Disk spill occurs when partition data exceeds available memory; increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` or executor memory

questions.shortAnswer: Spill to disk happens when a partition's data cannot fit in memory. Either increase shuffle partitions (smaller partitions) or executor memory (more room per partition). Reducing partitions makes the problem worse. CPU cores don't affect memory spill. OPTIMIZE affects file sizes, not in-memory partition sizes.

questions.title: Liquid Clustering
questions.question: A table currently uses `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (region, date)` which must be run manually after each batch load. The team wants automatic incremental data layout optimization. What is the correct approach to migrate to liquid clustering?

choices.A: `ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY (region, date)` and future writes/OPTIMIZE runs apply clustering incrementally
choices.B: `ALTER TABLE t SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.liquidClustering' = true, 'clusterColumns' = 'region,date')`
choices.C: Drop and recreate the table with `CREATE TABLE t CLUSTER BY (region, date)` using CTAS
choices.D: Liquid clustering and Z-ORDER cannot coexist; the table must be fully rewritten first

questions.shortAnswer: `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY` enables liquid clustering on an existing table. Future writes and OPTIMIZE runs will incrementally cluster data without rewriting the entire table. Option B uses incorrect syntax. Option C loses table history unnecessarily. Liquid clustering replaces Z-ORDER; they don't need to coexist since liquid clustering is incremental.

questions.title: Query Optimization with Predicate Pushdown
questions.question: A query reads from a Delta table partitioned by `date` and filtered by `region`. The EXPLAIN plan shows a `Filter` node above the `Scan` node for the `region` predicate. How can predicate pushdown for the `region` column be improved?

choices.A: Add a WHERE clause earlier in the SQL query to force pushdown
choices.B: Enable `spark.sql.optimizer.enablePredicatePushDown = true` (disabled by default)
choices.C: Apply Z-ORDER or liquid clustering on `region` to enable data skipping via file-level statistics
choices.D: Convert the `region` column to a partition column for physical-level pushdown

questions.shortAnswer: Delta Lake uses file-level min/max statistics for data skipping. Z-ORDER or liquid clustering by `region` co-locates similar values, making file statistics effective for skipping irrelevant files. Predicate pushdown is enabled by default. Query order doesn't affect pushdown. While partitioning by `region` works, it's not always advisable if cardinality is very high. Data skipping with Z-ORDER/clustering is the better approach for non-partition columns.

questions.title: Auto Optimize Settings
questions.question: A streaming pipeline writes to a Delta table using `foreachBatch`. The table accumulates many small files between manual OPTIMIZE runs. The team wants to automate file compaction. Which combination of settings prevents small file accumulation for this use case?

choices.A: Set `spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.enabled = true` only
choices.B: Set `spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled = true` only
choices.C: Enable both auto compaction and optimize write on the SparkSession
choices.D: Set both `delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite` and `delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact` as table properties

questions.shortAnswer: Setting both as table properties ensures they persist regardless of cluster configuration. `optimizeWrite` bins data during writes for better sizes. `autoCompact` runs a lightweight OPTIMIZE after writes. Using table properties (`ALTER TABLE SET TBLPROPERTIES`) is more reliable than SparkSession configs which must be set on every cluster/session.

questions.title: Reading Row-Level Changes *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Delta table has `delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true`. A downstream process must incrementally handle only rows that were updated or deleted since its last run, using the new values for updated rows, without scanning the whole table. Which approach is most efficient?

choices.A: Read with `.option("readChangeFeed", "true")` from the last processed version and keep rows where `_change_type` is `update_postimage` or `delete`
choices.B: Read with `readChangeFeed` and keep rows where `_change_type` is `update_preimage`
choices.C: Compare the current table with `VERSION AS OF` the previous version using a full anti-join
choices.D: Run `DESCRIBE HISTORY` and reprocess the full table whenever a new version exists

questions.shortAnswer: The change data feed returns only the changed rows; `update_postimage` carries the values after an update and `delete` marks removed rows.
questions.explanation: B is wrong because `update_preimage` holds the values before the update. C works but scans both versions in full, which defeats incremental processing. D reprocesses everything and gives no row-level change information.

questions.title: CDF and Retention *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A stream that reads a Delta table's change data feed was paused for six weeks. The table uses default retention settings and is vacuumed regularly. When restarted from a new checkpoint with `startingVersion` set to the last version it processed, the stream fails to start. What is the most likely cause?

choices.A: Change data feed is disabled automatically whenever `VACUUM` runs
choices.B: `readChangeFeed` works only for batch reads, not streaming reads
choices.C: The requested version and its change data are no longer in the table history; `VACUUM` removed the change files and log retention (default 30 days) expired the version
choices.D: `OPTIMIZE` renamed the `_change_type` column, breaking the stream schema

questions.shortAnswer: CDF is not a permanent record: change data follows the table's retention, and a stream cannot start from a version that is no longer in history.
questions.explanation: A is wrong because `VACUUM` deletes old files but does not turn off the table property. B is wrong because CDF supports streaming reads, and streaming is the recommended way to consume it. D is wrong because `OPTIMIZE` does not rename CDF metadata columns. The fix is to restart from an available version, and to archive the change feed if a long history is required.

questions.title: Retiring Maintenance Jobs *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team owns 40 external Delta tables registered in Unity Catalog. Every night an all-purpose cluster runs notebooks that execute `OPTIMIZE`, `VACUUM`, and `ANALYZE TABLE` on each table, and the team spends hours tuning the schedule. Predictive optimization is enabled at the account level. They want the platform to handle this maintenance automatically with the least ongoing effort. What should they do?

choices.A: Run `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION` on each external table and keep the nightly notebooks as a fallback
choices.B: Enable auto compaction on every table and move the notebooks to a job cluster to lower the DBU rate
choices.C: Convert the tables to Unity Catalog managed tables with `ALTER TABLE ... SET MANAGED`, let them inherit predictive optimization, and remove the scheduled maintenance jobs
choices.D: Add `ZORDER BY` to the nightly `OPTIMIZE` statements so that fewer runs are needed

questions.shortAnswer: Convert the tables to UC managed tables and let predictive optimization run `OPTIMIZE`, `VACUUM`, and `ANALYZE` automatically.
questions.explanation: Predictive optimization only supports Unity Catalog managed tables; it runs maintenance on serverless jobs compute when it is cost-effective, and Databricks recommends disabling scheduled `OPTIMIZE` jobs once it is on. `SET MANAGED` keeps the table name, permissions, and history. A is wrong because predictive optimization does not run on external tables, whatever the table-level setting. B still leaves the team owning `VACUUM` and statistics jobs. D adds work: Z-order must be re-applied manually and predictive optimization never runs `ZORDER`.

questions.title: Predictive Optimization Inheritance *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: Predictive optimization is enabled for the account. An admin runs `ALTER CATALOG finance DISABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION;` and later `ALTER SCHEMA finance.reporting ENABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION;`. No table-level settings exist, and all tables are Unity Catalog managed tables. Which statement describes the result?

choices.A: Managed tables in `finance.reporting` are maintained by predictive optimization, while managed tables in other `finance` schemas are not
choices.B: No tables in the `finance` catalog are maintained, because a catalog-level `DISABLE` overrides every schema below it
choices.C: All tables in `finance` are maintained, because the account-level setting always takes precedence
choices.D: Only tables created after the schema-level `ENABLE` are maintained; existing tables must be re-created

questions.shortAnswer: The schema-level `ENABLE` overrides the catalog's `DISABLE` for `finance.reporting`, and the other schemas inherit the catalog's `DISABLE`.
questions.explanation: Predictive optimization uses an inheritance model: account → catalog → schema → table, where an explicit `ENABLE` or `DISABLE` at a lower level overrides its parent and `INHERIT` resets it. B is wrong because lower levels can override the catalog. C is wrong because the account value is only the default that objects inherit. D is wrong because the setting applies to existing managed tables in the schema; no re-creation is needed.

questions.title: Changing Filter Patterns *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A 30 TB Unity Catalog managed gold table is queried by hundreds of analysts. One quarter most queries filter on `region`, the next on `product_id` and `order_date`, and the platform team has no time to keep re-tuning the layout. Predictive optimization is enabled for the catalog. Which approach best fits this access pattern?

choices.A: Partition the table by `region` and run a nightly `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (product_id, order_date)`
choices.B: Enable deletion vectors so that layout changes are applied at read time
choices.C: Define liquid clustering with all five frequently filtered columns as keys and run `OPTIMIZE FULL` every night
choices.D: Run `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY AUTO` so that predictive optimization selects and evolves the clustering keys from the query workload

questions.shortAnswer: `CLUSTER BY AUTO` lets predictive optimization choose clustering keys from the table's query history and change them as patterns shift.
questions.explanation: Automatic liquid clustering is available for UC managed tables with predictive optimization; it analyzes the historical query workload and changes keys only when the expected data-skipping savings outweigh the clustering cost. A hard-codes one pattern, needs manual Z-order runs, and partitioning is not recommended under 100 TB. B is wrong because deletion vectors reduce write amplification for row-level changes; they do not cluster data. C is invalid because liquid clustering allows at most four keys, and nightly `OPTIMIZE FULL` is unnecessary since clustering is incremental.

questions.title: Physically Removing Deleted Rows *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A customer table has deletion vectors enabled because it receives frequent small `MERGE` and `DELETE` operations. For a GDPR request, the engineer runs `DELETE FROM main.crm.customers WHERE customer_id = 42`. The compliance team requires that the deleted record's bytes no longer exist in any data file in storage. What should the engineer do next?

choices.A: Run `VACUUM` with the default retention; it removes soft-deleted rows from current data files
choices.B: Run `REORG TABLE main.crm.customers APPLY (PURGE)`, then run `VACUUM` so the old files from earlier table versions are removed
choices.C: Run `OPTIMIZE main.crm.customers ZORDER BY (customer_id)`, which guarantees every deletion vector is applied
choices.D: Disable deletion vectors with `ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = false)`, which rewrites the affected files immediately

questions.shortAnswer: `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` rewrites files that contain soft-deleted rows, and `VACUUM` then deletes the older files that still hold the data.
questions.explanation: With deletion vectors, a `DELETE` only marks the row in metadata, so the bytes stay in the existing Parquet file. The docs say to run `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` and then `VACUUM` to physically remove old data. A is wrong because `VACUUM` only deletes files no longer referenced by the table; the current file with the soft-deleted row is still referenced. C is wrong because compaction gives no strict guarantee that every deletion-vector change is applied. D is wrong because changing the property affects future writes; it does not purge existing soft-deleted data.

questions.title: Speeding Up Repeated Reads *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: Analysts on a classic all-purpose cluster run many different queries against the same few Delta tables throughout the day. Each query reads the data again from cloud object storage, and the team wants repeated reads to be faster without changing any notebook code. What should they do?

choices.A: Add `df.cache()` after every `spark.read.table()` call in the notebooks
choices.B: Run `CACHE SELECT * FROM` each table at the start of the day
choices.C: Choose a worker instance type with local SSDs so the disk (Delta) cache is enabled and stores copies of the Parquet files locally after the first read
choices.D: Increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` so that more tasks read from storage in parallel

questions.shortAnswer: Use SSD-backed workers so the disk cache automatically keeps local copies of the data files.
questions.explanation: The disk cache (formerly Delta cache) is enabled by default on worker types that support it; when a node fetches a Parquet file, it stores a copy on local storage, so later reads of the same data, from any query, run locally. A requires code changes and caches DataFrames manually in memory; Databricks recommends the disk cache instead of the Spark cache for repeated reads of Parquet and Delta data. B is wrong because `CACHE SELECT` is ignored on Databricks Runtime 14.2 and above and on SQL warehouses. D affects shuffle parallelism, not how often files are fetched from object storage.

questions.title: Disk Cache Consistency *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A cluster with the disk cache enabled has been serving dashboard queries on a Delta table for hours. A job then runs a `MERGE` that rewrites several of the table's files. A data engineer worries that the dashboards will keep returning old data from the cache. What happens?

choices.A: The cache keeps serving the old files until someone runs `CLEAR CACHE` on the cluster
choices.B: The cluster must be restarted to clear the local SSD cache
choices.C: The disk cache only stores query results, so the dashboards show old results until the 24-hour cache life cycle ends
choices.D: The disk cache detects that the data files were modified, invalidates the stale entries, and later reads return the current data with no manual action

questions.shortAnswer: The disk cache keeps itself consistent by detecting created, deleted, modified, or overwritten files.
questions.explanation: The docs state that you can write, modify, and delete table data with no need to explicitly invalidate cached data; stale entries are invalidated and evicted automatically. A and B describe manual invalidation that the disk cache does not require (restarting only clears it). C confuses the disk cache, which stores data files, with the Databricks SQL result cache; the result cache has a 24-hour life cycle but is also invalidated when the underlying tables are updated.

questions.title: Stats Unused in the Query Profile *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A SQL warehouse query filters a large liquid-clustered table with `WHERE CAST(event_date AS STRING) = '2026-10-01'`, and `event_date` is a clustering key. The query profile shows the Scan operator taking most of the time, a low percentage of data pruned, and a `COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA` insight with the status Unused. What is the best fix?

choices.A: Increase the warehouse size so the full scan finishes faster
choices.B: Rewrite the predicate to compare the column directly, for example `WHERE event_date = DATE'2026-10-01'`
choices.C: Add a `/*+ BROADCAST */` hint to the query
choices.D: Run `SET use_cached_result = false` so the profile reflects a fresh execution

questions.shortAnswer: Compare `event_date` directly so its min/max statistics can be used for file skipping.
questions.explanation: The `COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA` insight reports Unused when statistics can't be used because the filter converts the data type; data skipping relies on per-file min/max values of the column itself. A treats the symptom and costs more without restoring skipping. C is about join strategy and the query has no join problem. D only bypasses the result cache; it doesn't change how many files are read.

questions.title: Missed Broadcast Join *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A query joins a 2 TB fact table to a 5 MB country dimension on `country_code`. In the query profile, Shuffle operators feed both inputs of the Join, and the Shuffle on the fact side has the highest Time spent and Memory peak. The dimension table has no optimizer statistics. What change most directly removes the expensive shuffle of the fact table?

choices.A: Increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` so each shuffle partition is smaller
choices.B: Add a `/*+ MERGE(d) */` hint so the join uses a sort-merge join
choices.C: Add a `/*+ BROADCAST(d) */` hint on the dimension (or collect statistics with `ANALYZE TABLE`) so the small side is broadcast and the fact table is not shuffled
choices.D: Z-order the fact table by `country_code`

questions.shortAnswer: Broadcasting the small dimension avoids shuffling the 2 TB fact table.
questions.explanation: Shuffle operators on both join inputs mean a shuffled join; in a broadcast hash join the small side is sent to every executor and the large side isn't shuffled. The `BROADCAST` hint broadcasts the hinted side regardless of `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, and missing or stale statistics (the `COVERAGE_STATS_OPTIMIZER` insight) lead to wrong size estimates and a slow join strategy. A only resizes the shuffle; the fact table is still moved across the network. B forces a strategy that also shuffles (and sorts) both sides. D improves file skipping for filters, not the join's data movement.

questions.title: Small Table, Many Partitions *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A 400 GB orders table is partitioned by `order_date`, which has produced thousands of small partitions. Most queries filter on `customer_id` (millions of distinct values) and a date range. The team wants the layout Databricks currently recommends for this size and query pattern. What should they choose?

choices.A: Re-partition the table by `customer_id` to match the most common filter
choices.B: Keep the date partitioning and schedule a nightly `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (customer_id)`
choices.C: Keep the date partitioning and add a Bloom filter index on `customer_id`
choices.D: Remove the partitioning and use liquid clustering on `order_date` and `customer_id`

questions.shortAnswer: Drop partitioning and cluster the table on the filter columns with liquid clustering.
questions.explanation: Databricks says tables under 1 TB should not be partitioned, recommends liquid clustering for all new tables, and notes that liquid clustering works for both low- and high-cardinality columns without the small-file issues of static partitioning. A is worse: partitioning only suits low or known cardinality, and millions of `customer_id` values would create millions of tiny partitions. B keeps the over-partitioned layout and adds a manual Z-order job that predictive optimization never maintains. C is wrong because Bloom filter indexes are deprecated and superseded by predictive I/O and liquid clustering.

questions.title: Migrating a Partitioned, Z-Ordered Table *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A 60 TB Delta table is partitioned by `event_date` and Z-ordered nightly by `device_id`. The team wants to move to liquid clustering with minimal reader and writer downtime while keeping data skipping on both columns, using Databricks Runtime 18.1. Which approach should they use?

choices.A: Run `ALTER TABLE events REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY (event_date, device_id)` and then run `OPTIMIZE`
choices.B: Run `ALTER TABLE events CLUSTER BY (device_id)` on the partitioned table and keep the nightly Z-order job
choices.C: Create a new table with both `PARTITIONED BY (event_date)` and `CLUSTER BY (device_id)` using CTAS
choices.D: Run `OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, device_id)` once, which converts the table to liquid clustering

questions.shortAnswer: Use the in-place `REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY` conversion with the partition and Z-order columns as keys, then `OPTIMIZE`.
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends this conversion (DBR 18.1+) because it minimizes reader and writer downtime, and its migration guidance says to use both the partition columns and the `ZORDER BY` columns as clustering keys; running `OPTIMIZE` afterwards applies the new clustering. B is wrong because `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY` enables liquid clustering only on unpartitioned tables, and liquid clustering is incompatible with `ZORDER`. C is invalid because clustering is not compatible with partitioning. D only rewrites files with Z-order; it never enables liquid clustering.

questions.title: Row-Level Security
questions.question: Different sales teams should only see data for their assigned regions. Which approach implements row-level security in Unity Catalog?

choices.A: Create separate tables for each region
choices.B: Use dynamic views with `current_user()` function
choices.C: Apply column masking policies
choices.D: Use secret scopes for each region

questions.shortAnswer: Dynamic views using `current_user()` or `is_member()` functions filter rows based on the querying user's identity or group membership. Column masking hides column values. Separate tables don't scale. Secret scopes are for credentials.

questions.title: Secret Management
questions.question: A notebook needs to access a database password without exposing it in code. Which approach correctly retrieves the secret?

choices.A: `dbutils.secrets.get(scope="db-scope", key="password")`
choices.B: `spark.conf.get("db.password")`
choices.C: `dbutils.credentials.get("db-scope", "password")`
choices.D: `os.environ.get("DB_PASSWORD")`

questions.shortAnswer: `dbutils.secrets.get(scope, key)` retrieves secrets from Databricks secret scopes. The value is automatically redacted in notebook output. The other options either don't exist or expose credentials.

questions.title: Data Lineage
questions.question: An audit team needs to understand how a Gold-layer table is derived from raw data sources, including all intermediate transformations. How does Unity Catalog capture this lineage information?

choices.A: Lineage is automatically captured from Spark jobs, Lakeflow pipelines, and SQL queries without additional configuration
choices.B: Engineers must manually register lineage by calling `dbutils.lineage.register()` after each transformation
choices.C: Lineage is only available for Lakeflow pipelines, not for general Spark jobs
choices.D: Lineage requires enabling a separate "Lineage Tracking" feature at the metastore level

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog automatically captures column-level and table-level lineage from Spark operations, Lakeflow pipelines, and SQL queries. No manual registration is needed. The lineage is available in the Catalog Explorer UI and via REST API. It works across notebooks, jobs, and Lakeflow pipelines.

questions.title: Audit Logging
questions.question: A security team needs to investigate who accessed a sensitive table in the last 30 days and what queries they ran. Which system table provides this information?

choices.A: `system.information_schema.tables` - contains table metadata including last access time
choices.B: `system.billing.usage` - tracks DBU consumption per user and table
choices.C: `system.access.audit` - records all access events including user, action, and resource
choices.D: `system.compute.clusters` - logs cluster activity and associated table access

questions.shortAnswer: `system.access.audit` is the system table that records all access events in Unity Catalog, including who accessed which resources, what actions were performed, and when. Information schema has metadata, not access history. Billing tracks costs. Compute tables track cluster lifecycle.

questions.title: Column Masking
questions.question: A table contains PII (email, phone number). Analysts need to query the table but should only see masked versions of PII columns unless they are in the `pii_readers` group. Which Unity Catalog feature implements this requirement?

choices.A: Create a dynamic view that checks `is_member('pii_readers')` and conditionally shows full or masked values
choices.B: Create separate tables with and without PII, granting access to the appropriate one
choices.C: Use `DENY SELECT` on PII columns for non-PII readers
choices.D: Apply column mask functions using `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK`

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog column masking (`SET MASK`) applies a function that controls what value each user sees based on their identity or group membership. This is applied directly to the table, not requiring separate views or tables. `DENY SELECT` on individual columns is not supported in Unity Catalog. Dynamic views work but column masking is the more direct, recommended approach.

questions.title: Network Security
questions.question: A financial services company requires that all Databricks workspace traffic stays within their private network and never traverses the public internet. Which network configuration achieves this?

choices.A: Enable IP access lists to restrict source IP addresses
choices.B: Configure VPN peering between the corporate network and Databricks control plane
choices.C: Deploy a workspace with Private Link / Private Endpoints for both front-end and back-end connectivity
choices.D: Use a firewall to block all outbound traffic from the Databricks data plane

questions.shortAnswer: Private Link (AWS) / Private Endpoints (Azure) ensure both the front-end (UI/API) and back-end (data plane to control plane) connections remain on the private network backbone without traversing the public internet. IP access lists restrict who can access but still use public internet. VPN alone doesn't cover all connection paths. Blocking outbound breaks Databricks functionality.

questions.title: GDPR Compliance - Right to Erasure
questions.question: Under GDPR, a customer requests deletion of all their personal data. The customer's data exists in Bronze, Silver, and Gold Delta tables across the lakehouse. What is the correct approach to fulfill this deletion request?

choices.A: Run `VACUUM` on all tables to remove files containing the customer's data
choices.B: Use time travel to revert each table to a version before the customer's data was ingested
choices.C: Delete the customer's records only from Gold tables since Bronze/Silver are considered raw storage exempt from GDPR
choices.D: Execute `DELETE FROM` on all tables containing the customer's data, then `VACUUM` to physically remove the old files

questions.shortAnswer: GDPR right to erasure requires physical deletion. First, `DELETE FROM` marks records as removed in Delta's transaction log. Then `VACUUM` removes the old files that still contain the deleted data. All tables (including Bronze/Silver) must be processed - GDPR applies regardless of data tier. Time travel would lose all other changes. VACUUM alone doesn't target specific records.

questions.title: Least-Privilege Job Operators *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An on-call support group must be able to trigger, cancel, and repair runs of a production Lakeflow job and read its run logs, but must not be able to edit the job's tasks or change its permissions. Which job permission level should the group receive?

choices.A: CAN VIEW
choices.B: CAN MANAGE
choices.C: CAN MANAGE RUN
choices.D: IS OWNER

questions.shortAnswer: CAN MANAGE RUN is the least-privilege level that allows running, cancelling, and viewing run logs without editing the job.
questions.explanation: CAN MANAGE RUN allows Run now, Run now with different parameters, cancel, and viewing Spark UI and logs, but not editing job settings, deleting, or modifying permissions. CAN VIEW only shows job details and results. CAN MANAGE and IS OWNER both add editing, deleting, and permission changes, which violates least privilege, and a group cannot be IS OWNER of a job.

questions.title: Data Grants vs Workspace ACLs *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: Analysts must run ad hoc queries on the `prod.gold` schema through a shared SQL warehouse, with no ability to change the warehouse or modify data. Which combination follows least privilege?

choices.A: CAN MANAGE on the warehouse and `ALL PRIVILEGES` on `prod.gold`
choices.B: CAN USE on the warehouse, plus `USE CATALOG` on `prod` and `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT` on `prod.gold`
choices.C: CAN USE on the warehouse and `SELECT` on `prod.gold` only
choices.D: IS OWNER on the warehouse and `MODIFY` on `prod.gold`

questions.shortAnswer: CAN USE on the warehouse plus `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, and `SELECT` is the minimal combination.
questions.explanation: Workspace ACLs control the warehouse (CAN USE lets users start it and run queries) while Unity Catalog grants control data; reading a table requires the usage privileges on the parent catalog and schema plus `SELECT`. Option C fails because `SELECT` without `USE CATALOG` causes permission denied. Options A and D grant editing rights on the warehouse and write access to data.

questions.title: Choosing ABAC for Future Tables *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A governance team must mask every column tagged `pii : ssn` in all current and future tables of the `hr` catalog, and table owners must not be able to remove the masking. What should they implement?

choices.A: A column mask policy created with `CREATE POLICY ... ON CATALOG hr COLUMN MASK ... MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('pii', 'ssn')`
choices.B: `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ssn SET MASK` on every existing table
choices.C: A dynamic view per table that hashes the SSN column
choices.D: A row filter function attached to each schema in the catalog

questions.shortAnswer: An ABAC column mask policy at the catalog level, matching the governed tag, covers current and future tables centrally.
questions.explanation: ABAC policies are evaluated dynamically for every table in scope whose columns carry the matching governed tag, and table owners cannot modify or bypass a policy set at a higher level. Per-table `SET MASK` does not cover future tables and table owners can remove it. Dynamic views require new objects and users could still query base tables if granted. A row filter hides rows, not column values.

questions.title: ABAC Permissions and Tag Scope *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A schema-level ABAC column mask policy uses `MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('pii') AS c ON COLUMN c`. A steward tags the table `customers` with `pii` but not its columns, and queries still return unmasked values. What is the cause?

choices.A: The policy creator lacks `SELECT` on the table
choices.B: Column conditions in `MATCH COLUMNS` match only tags set directly on columns; table tags do not propagate to columns
choices.C: ABAC policies only apply to tables created after the policy
choices.D: The `pii` tag must be ungoverned for ABAC to use it

questions.shortAnswer: `MATCH COLUMNS` checks column-level tags only, so the column itself must be tagged.
questions.explanation: `has_tag()` in `WHEN` considers table tags and tags inherited from the schema or catalog, but in `MATCH COLUMNS` it checks tags applied directly on the column; tags never inherit to columns. Policies apply to existing and future tables, and ABAC works only with governed tags. Creating a policy requires `MANAGE` on the scope and `EXECUTE` on the UDF, not `SELECT`.

questions.title: Pseudonymization for Joins *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: Analysts need to join orders, support tickets, and web events by customer without ever seeing customer email addresses, and the same customer must map to the same value in every table. Which technique fits best?

choices.A: Suppression: replace email with `NULL` in all tables
choices.B: Generalization: keep only the email domain
choices.C: Pseudonymization: store `sha2(concat(<secret salt>, lower(email)), 256)` as the join key
choices.D: Random tokens generated with `uuid()` independently in each table

questions.shortAnswer: A salted deterministic hash pseudonymizes the email while keeping it joinable across tables.
questions.explanation: `sha2` produces the same output for the same input, so the hashed key joins across tables, and the secret salt prevents dictionary reversal of low-entropy values. Suppression and generalization remove the ability to join individual customers. Independent `uuid()` values differ per table unless managed through a single token vault.

questions.title: Anonymization vs Pseudonymization *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: Which transformation is an anonymization technique rather than a pseudonymization technique?

choices.A: Replacing exact ages with ten-year age bands and ZIP codes with their first three digits
choices.B: Replacing emails with tokens stored in a restricted lookup table
choices.C: Encrypting SSNs with `aes_encrypt` using a key from a secret scope
choices.D: Hashing customer IDs with a salted `sha2`

questions.shortAnswer: Generalization (age bands, truncated ZIP codes) coarsens data irreversibly, which is anonymization.
questions.explanation: Tokenization, encryption, and salted hashing keep records linkable and can be reversed or re-linked with additional information (vault, key, or salt), so they are pseudonymization techniques.

questions.title: Automated PII Detection and Masking *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: New source feeds land in a catalog every week through batch jobs and Lakeflow streaming tables. The company wants sensitive columns detected and masked automatically without engineers tagging each new column. Which approach uses Unity Catalog features to achieve this?

choices.A: Ask engineers to add AI-generated comments to every new table and mask columns whose comment mentions PII
choices.B: Enable Data Classification with auto-tagging on the catalog and create an ABAC column mask policy on the catalog that matches the `class.*` tags
choices.C: Write a regex UDF in each pipeline and apply it before writing every table
choices.D: Create a dynamic view over each new table after it is published

questions.shortAnswer: Data Classification auto-tags detected PII columns with `class.*` system tags, and a catalog-level ABAC policy masks them for all table types.
questions.explanation: Data Classification incrementally scans tables, streaming tables, and materialized views, and ABAC policies apply to all tables in scope, so new feeds are covered automatically for batch and streaming consumers. Databricks states AI-generated comments should not be relied on to detect PII. Per-pipeline regex and dynamic views require manual work for each new table.

questions.title: Pipeline Identity and Masked Refreshes *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: After a catalog-level ABAC column mask policy `TO account users` is created, a Lakeflow pipeline refreshes a gold materialized view from masked silver tables, and every user, including privacy officers, now sees masked values in the materialized view. What is the correct fix?

choices.A: Grant `SELECT` on the materialized view to the privacy officers
choices.B: Add the pipeline owner or run-as service principal to the policy's `EXCEPT` clause and fully refresh the materialized view
choices.C: Disable deletion vectors on the materialized view
choices.D: Move the policy from the catalog to each table

questions.shortAnswer: The pipeline identity must be exempt so the refresh reads unmasked source data.
questions.explanation: Pipelines evaluate policies with the pipeline owner or run-as identity during refresh, so a masked identity permanently stores masked data in the materialized view; exempting it via `EXCEPT` and refreshing fixes the stored data while consumers remain covered by policies. Extra grants do not unmask stored values, deletion vectors are unrelated, and table-level policies would reproduce the same problem.

questions.title: Erasure with Deletion Vectors *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A table has deletion vectors enabled. To satisfy a right-to-erasure request, an engineer runs `DELETE FROM users WHERE user_id = 42`. Which additional steps physically remove the user's data from storage?

choices.A: `OPTIMIZE users` immediately, which guarantees removal
choices.B: `REORG TABLE users APPLY (PURGE)`, then `VACUUM users` after the old files exceed the retention threshold
choices.C: `VACUUM users` immediately; deletion vectors are removed by `VACUUM`
choices.D: `RESTORE TABLE users` to the version before the delete

questions.shortAnswer: `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` rewrites files containing soft-deleted rows, and `VACUUM` later deletes the old files.
questions.explanation: With deletion vectors, `DELETE` only marks rows as removed; `APPLY (PURGE)` rewrites the affected files, but older files remain for time travel until `VACUUM` removes them after they expire under `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration`. `OPTIMIZE` compaction gives no strict guarantee of applying deletion vectors, `VACUUM` alone does not rewrite current files, and `RESTORE` brings the data back.

questions.title: Retention on Databricks Runtime 18 *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: On Databricks Runtime 18.0, an engineer runs `VACUUM events RETAIN 72 HOURS` to shorten the purge window for a compliance requirement, but files older than 72 hours are not removed. What should they do?

choices.A: Run `VACUUM events RETAIN 72 HOURS DRY RUN` first
choices.B: Set `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` on the table to the required interval and run `VACUUM`
choices.C: Increase `delta.logRetentionDuration` to 365 days
choices.D: Disable predictive optimization

questions.shortAnswer: In Databricks Runtime 18.0+, retention is controlled by the `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` table property.
questions.explanation: The Runtime 18.0 release notes state that `VACUUM` ignores the retention argument except for `0 HOURS`, and that `deletedFileRetentionDuration` and `logRetentionDuration` must be consistent. `DRY RUN` only lists files, increasing log retention lengthens history, and disabling predictive optimization stops automatic `VACUUM` instead of purging sooner.

questions.title: Unity Catalog Volumes vs DBFS
questions.question: A team needs to store raw data files that will be governed by Unity Catalog. Which storage option should they use?

choices.A: DBFS root storage
choices.B: Mounted cloud storage
choices.C: Unity Catalog Volume
choices.D: Workspace files

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog Volumes provide governed file storage with access controls, auditing, and lineage. DBFS and mounts are legacy approaches without UC governance. Workspace files are for notebooks and small files, not data.

questions.title: Unity Catalog Permission Inheritance
questions.question: A user is granted SELECT on a schema in Unity Catalog. What happens to tables created in that schema after the grant?

choices.A: User automatically has SELECT on new tables
choices.B: User must be granted SELECT on each new table
choices.C: User has no access to new tables
choices.D: User has MODIFY access to new tables

questions.shortAnswer: Permissions in Unity Catalog inherit downward. A SELECT grant on a schema applies to all current and future tables in that schema. This simplifies access management compared to table-level grants.

questions.title: Managed vs External Tables
questions.question: A team needs to register an existing data lake path in Unity Catalog without moving the data. What type of table should they create?

choices.A: Managed table
choices.B: External table
choices.C: View
choices.D: Materialized view

questions.shortAnswer: External tables point to data at a user-specified location. Managed tables store data in Unity Catalog-managed storage (data would be moved/copied). Views don't store data. Materialized views persist computed results.

questions.title: Information Schema
questions.question: A data governance team needs to programmatically inventory all tables across all catalogs that a service principal has access to, including their column types and descriptions. Which query approach provides this information?

choices.A: Query `system.information_schema.columns` which shows metadata for all accessible objects
choices.B: Run `SHOW TABLES IN *` to list all tables across catalogs
choices.C: Use `dbutils.fs.ls()` to scan the metastore storage location
choices.D: Call the Unity Catalog REST API endpoint `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/tables`

questions.shortAnswer: `system.information_schema.columns` provides metadata about all columns in all tables the current user/principal can access. It includes column names, types, descriptions, and table ownership. `SHOW TABLES` works per-schema only. `dbutils.fs.ls()` shows files, not metadata. The REST API works but requires pagination and more code.

questions.title: Data Classification Tags
questions.question: An organization needs to tag tables and columns containing sensitive data (PII, financial, health) to enforce governance policies and improve discoverability. How should data classification be implemented in Unity Catalog?

choices.A: Store classification metadata in a separate governance database and cross-reference during queries
choices.B: Use Unity Catalog tags (`ALTER TABLE ... SET TAGS`) to apply classification labels at table and column level
choices.C: Add `COMMENT` on each column with classification keywords and search comments for enforcement
choices.D: Create a naming convention (e.g., `pii_email`, `sensitive_ssn`) and enforce via CI/CD checks

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog tags provide first-class support for classifying tables and columns. Tags are searchable in Catalog Explorer, can be queried via information schema, and integrate with governance workflows. Comments are free-text and harder to enforce programmatically. Naming conventions are fragile. Separate databases add complexity.

questions.title: Tags vs Comments *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A data steward wants analysts to find all tables belonging to the finance team through workspace search filters and also give each table a human-readable description. Which combination is appropriate?

choices.A: Comments for both purposes
choices.B: A tag such as `team = finance` for filtering, and `COMMENT ON TABLE` for the description
choices.C: Table properties set with `TBLPROPERTIES` for both purposes
choices.D: A row filter that returns only finance rows

questions.shortAnswer: Tags are key-value attributes suited to filtering and searching, while comments hold free-text descriptions.
questions.explanation: Workspace search supports `tag:<key>:<value>` and tag filters, and also indexes table and column comments. Comments alone do not give structured filtering, table properties are not the discovery mechanism, and row filters restrict data access rather than add metadata.

questions.title: Discoverability Without Data Access *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: All employees should be able to see that tables in the `sales` catalog exist, including their names, comments, and tags, and request access, without being able to read any data. Which grant achieves this?

choices.A: `GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales` to the account users group
choices.B: `GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG sales` to the account users group
choices.C: `GRANT BROWSE ON CATALOG sales` to the account users group
choices.D: `GRANT APPLY TAG ON CATALOG sales` to the account users group

questions.shortAnswer: `BROWSE` exposes object metadata and access requests without data access.
questions.explanation: `BROWSE` is granted at the catalog level and lets users discover objects and view names, descriptions, and tags without `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, or `SELECT`. `SELECT` grants data access, `USE CATALOG` alone is only a prerequisite, and `APPLY TAG` lets users change tags.

questions.title: Inheritance to New Tables *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An administrator grants `USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT` on catalog `sales` to the `finance_team` group. A week later, a new schema `sales.forecast` and a table `sales.forecast.q4` are created. Assuming no other grants, what can `finance_team` do with `sales.forecast.q4`?

choices.A: Nothing until `SELECT` is granted on the new table
choices.B: Query it, because privileges granted on a catalog are inherited by current and future schemas and tables
choices.C: Query it only if they also own the new schema
choices.D: Modify and drop it, because catalog grants imply ownership

questions.shortAnswer: Catalog-level privileges inherit downward to all current and future child objects.
questions.explanation: Because `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, and `SELECT` were granted on the catalog, they apply to every schema and table in it, including ones created later. No per-table grant is needed, ownership is unrelated to inherited privileges, and `SELECT` does not include `MODIFY` or drop rights.

questions.title: Ownership vs MANAGE *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A platform team wants a governance group to grant and revoke privileges on every table in `prod.gold`, including future tables, without making the group the owner and without giving it automatic read access to the data. What should they grant?

choices.A: `ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA prod.gold`
choices.B: `SELECT ON SCHEMA prod.gold WITH GRANT OPTION`
choices.C: `MANAGE ON SCHEMA prod.gold`
choices.D: Ownership of every table in `prod.gold`

questions.shortAnswer: `MANAGE` on the schema delegates grant management for the schema and all its current and future objects.
questions.explanation: `MANAGE` allows managing privileges, transferring ownership, and dropping objects without ownership and is inherited by child objects, but does not itself include data privileges. `ALL PRIVILEGES` grants data access and excludes `MANAGE`, Unity Catalog has no `WITH GRANT OPTION`, and transferring ownership of each table is not what was asked.

questions.title: Databricks CLI Authentication
questions.question: A CI/CD pipeline needs to authenticate with Databricks using a service principal. Which environment variables should be set?

choices.A: `DATABRICKS_HOST` and `DATABRICKS_TOKEN`
choices.B: `DATABRICKS_HOST`, `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID`, and `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET`
choices.C: `DATABRICKS_URL` and `DATABRICKS_API_KEY`
choices.D: `DATABRICKS_WORKSPACE` and `DATABRICKS_PAT`

questions.shortAnswer: Service principal authentication requires the workspace host URL, client ID (application ID), and client secret. Option A is for PAT token authentication. Options C and D use invalid variable names.

questions.title: Spark UI Debugging
questions.question: A Spark job is experiencing long task times with high "Shuffle Read Blocked Time." What does this indicate?

choices.A: Too few partitions
choices.B: Network congestion or slow shuffle fetch
choices.C: Out of memory errors
choices.D: Insufficient disk space

questions.shortAnswer: Shuffle Read Blocked Time indicates tasks waiting for shuffle data from other executors, typically due to network issues or executors being slow to serve shuffle blocks. Solutions include increasing shuffle retry settings or investigating network.

questions.title: Declarative Automation Bundles
questions.question: A team needs to deploy the same pipeline to dev, staging, and production environments. How should environments be configured in Declarative Automation Bundles?

choices.A: Create separate bundle files for each environment
choices.B: Use targets in databricks.yml with environment-specific settings
choices.C: Use Git branches for each environment
choices.D: Manually modify settings before each deployment

questions.shortAnswer: DAB uses targets to define environment-specific configurations in a single databricks.yml. This is the recommended approach for multi-environment deployments. Separate files or manual changes lead to drift and errors.

questions.title: Bundle Deployment Mode
questions.question: A developer wants to test their bundle without affecting shared resources. Which target mode should they use?

choices.A: `mode: production`
choices.B: `mode: development`
choices.C: `mode: testing`
choices.D: `mode: sandbox`

questions.shortAnswer: Development mode prefixes resource names with the username, pauses schedules, and uses personal workspace paths. This prevents conflicts with other developers or production resources.

questions.title: Git Folders
questions.question: A team wants to version control their notebooks with automatic sync to Git. Which statement about Git Folders is correct?

choices.A: Git Folders require manual sync after each change
choices.B: Git Folders can only connect to GitHub
choices.C: Git Folders replace the need for Declarative Automation Bundles
choices.D: Git Folders provide native Git operations like pull, commit, and push

questions.shortAnswer: Git Folders provide native Git operations directly in the Databricks UI. They support multiple Git providers (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, etc.). They complement DAB (which handles deployment), not replace it.

questions.title: CI/CD Pipeline
questions.question: A GitHub Actions workflow needs to deploy a bundle to Databricks. Which step is required before running `databricks bundle deploy`?

choices.A: Install Python
choices.B: Run `databricks bundle init`
choices.C: Set up Databricks CLI with authentication
choices.D: Create the workspace manually

questions.shortAnswer: The Databricks CLI must be installed and authenticated (via `databricks/setup-cli` action or environment variables) before deployment commands work. The bundle already exists in the repo. Python is helpful but CLI is essential.

questions.title: OIDC Federation for CI/CD
questions.question: A security team requires that CI/CD pipelines authenticate to Databricks without storing long-lived tokens in GitHub Actions secrets. What is the recommended authentication approach?

choices.A: Use OIDC federation with GitHub's identity provider so the pipeline exchanges a short-lived GitHub token for a Databricks access token
choices.B: Generate a personal access token (PAT) and store it as an encrypted GitHub secret with automatic rotation
choices.C: Use a service principal with a client secret stored in a vault and injected at runtime
choices.D: Configure SSH key-based authentication between GitHub Actions runners and the Databricks workspace

questions.shortAnswer: OIDC (OpenID Connect) federation allows GitHub Actions to authenticate to Databricks without storing any secrets. The pipeline receives a short-lived OIDC token from GitHub's identity provider and exchanges it for a Databricks token. This eliminates secret management entirely. PATs and client secrets still require secret storage and rotation. SSH authentication is not supported for Databricks API calls.

questions.title: Blue/Green Deployment
questions.question: A production pipeline processes financial data and cannot tolerate downtime during updates. The team needs a zero-downtime deployment strategy. How should a blue/green deployment be implemented with Declarative Automation Bundles?

choices.A: Deploy the new version to the same target and rely on Databricks to handle the transition automatically
choices.B: Maintain two separate DAB targets (blue and green), deploy the new version to the inactive target, run validation, then switch traffic
choices.C: Use `databricks bundle deploy --rolling` to gradually replace running tasks
choices.D: Deploy to a staging target, run all tests, then use `databricks bundle promote` to move to production

questions.shortAnswer: Blue/green deployment uses two parallel environments. Deploy to the inactive one, validate, then switch traffic (e.g., by updating a job alias or routing). This provides instant rollback by switching back. Databricks doesn't auto-handle transitions. There is no `--rolling` or `promote` command in the DAB CLI.

questions.title: Bundle Variable Substitution
questions.question: A DAB project needs different cluster sizes, catalog names, and notification emails for dev vs. production targets. Which approach correctly parameterizes these differences?

choices.A: Use shell environment variables like `$CLUSTER_SIZE` directly in databricks.yml
choices.B: Create separate databricks.yml files for each environment (databricks-dev.yml, databricks-prod.yml)
choices.C: Use Jinja2 templating syntax `{{ env.CLUSTER_SIZE }}` in the bundle configuration
choices.D: Define variables in the bundle and override them per target using `variables:` blocks with `${var.variable_name}` syntax

questions.shortAnswer: DAB supports native variable substitution with `${var.variable_name}` syntax. Variables are defined at the bundle level and can be overridden per target in the `targets:` section. Shell variables, separate files, and Jinja2 are not supported in DAB configuration syntax.

questions.title: Deployment Validation
questions.question: A deployment pipeline needs to verify that a bundle is correctly configured before deploying to production, checking for missing permissions, invalid references, and configuration errors. Which command performs this validation?

choices.A: `databricks bundle test -t production`
choices.B: `databricks bundle lint -t production`
choices.C: `databricks bundle validate -t production`
choices.D: `databricks bundle check -t production`

questions.shortAnswer: `databricks bundle validate` checks the bundle configuration for errors including missing resources, invalid references, schema validation, and permission issues. It should always run before `databricks bundle deploy`. There is no `test`, `lint`, or `check` subcommand in the DAB CLI.

questions.title: GitOps Workflow
questions.question: A team implements GitOps where the Git repository is the single source of truth. Changes to production should only occur through merged pull requests. How should the CI/CD pipeline enforce this GitOps principle?

choices.A: Allow direct deployments from any branch but require admin approval in the Databricks workspace
choices.B: Configure the deployment pipeline to only trigger on merges to the main branch, with PR reviews and bundle validation as required checks
choices.C: Use Git Folders to auto-sync the main branch to the production workspace
choices.D: Lock the production workspace to read-only and require API-only deployments

questions.shortAnswer: GitOps requires that all changes flow through Git. The CI/CD pipeline should only deploy from main branch (after PR merge), with validation and tests as required GitHub/GitLab checks before merge is allowed. Git Folders sync notebooks but don't handle full bundle deployment. Read-only workspaces break operational needs. Direct deployment from any branch bypasses review.

questions.title: Spark UI Stage Analysis
questions.question: A data engineer examines the Spark UI and notices one stage has 200 tasks where 199 complete in 2 seconds but 1 task takes 15 minutes. What is this pattern called and which AQE feature addresses it?

choices.A: A straggler task; enable speculative execution with `spark.speculation = true`
choices.B: Data skew; AQE's `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled` splits the skewed partition
choices.C: A scheduling delay; increase `spark.executor.cores` for faster task scheduling
choices.D: Garbage collection overhead; tune JVM GC with `spark.executor.extraJavaOptions`

questions.shortAnswer: One task taking much longer than others with the same data is classic data skew. AQE's skew join optimization detects skewed partitions and splits them into smaller sub-partitions. Speculative execution re-runs slow tasks but doesn't fix the root cause. This isn't a scheduling or GC issue.

questions.title: Diagnosing on Serverless *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A notebook task in a Lakeflow Jobs run on serverless compute became much slower after a code change, and the data engineer wants operator-level detail (time spent, rows, memory, pruning) for the slow statement. The compute page shows no Spark UI tab. Where should the engineer look?

choices.A: The Driver logs tab on the serverless compute
choices.B: The compute event log for the serverless compute
choices.C: The query profile for the statement, opened from the task's timeline in the job run (or from query history)
choices.D: Log delivery output in a Unity Catalog volume configured on the serverless compute

questions.shortAnswer: The query profile replaces the Spark UI for serverless workloads.
questions.explanation: Serverless compute does not provide the Spark UI or Spark logs; Databricks says to use the query profile, which shows per-operator time spent, rows, memory peak, and pruning, and serverless job runs list each statement in the task timeline with a link to its profile. A and D are wrong because Spark driver logs and compute log delivery are not available on serverless (only client-side application logs). B is wrong because compute event logs are not supported on serverless and only describe compute lifecycle, not query execution.

questions.title: Fleet-Wide Failure Analysis *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A platform team must find every job task that failed or timed out across all workspaces in the last week, grouped by failure reason, without opening each run in the UI. Which source gives this most directly?

choices.A: The Spark UI Jobs tab of each job cluster
choices.B: The `system.lakeflow.job_task_run_timeline` system table, filtered on `result_state` and grouped by `termination_code`
choices.C: The driver logs of each job cluster delivered to a volume
choices.D: The `system.billing.usage` system table filtered on failed SKUs

questions.shortAnswer: The `system.lakeflow.job_task_run_timeline` table records each task run's `result_state` and `termination_code` across the account.
questions.explanation: System tables are governed, queryable records with 365-day retention, so one SQL query can count `FAILED`, `ERROR`, and `TIMED_OUT` task runs by `termination_code` (for example `RUN_EXECUTION_ERROR` or `CLUSTER_ERROR`). A is per-application and disappears when compute is restarted. C requires parsing raw log files per cluster and does not give outcomes. D tracks usage and cost, not run outcomes.

questions.title: What a Repair Re-runs *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A job has tasks `ingest`, then `clean_a` and `clean_b` in parallel, then `publish` depending on both. In last night's run `ingest` and `clean_a` succeeded, `clean_b` failed, and `publish` was skipped. The engineer fixes the bug in `clean_b`'s notebook and clicks **Repair run** with default settings. What happens?

choices.A: All four tasks run again in a new job run with a new run ID
choices.B: Only `clean_b` runs again; `publish` must be triggered manually
choices.C: `clean_b` and `publish` run again as part of the original run, using the current job and task settings
choices.D: `ingest`, `clean_b`, and `publish` run again because repairs always restart from the first task

questions.shortAnswer: A repair re-runs only the unsuccessful tasks and their dependents, inside the original run.
questions.explanation: Repair re-runs the failed `clean_b` and the skipped dependent `publish`, does not re-run successful tasks (`ingest`, `clean_a`), uses the current job and task settings so the fix is picked up, and records the repair in the original run's history. A describes Run now, not repair. B ignores dependent tasks. D is wrong because successful tasks are not re-run.

questions.title: Repair with a Parameter Override via API *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A run that was already repaired once failed again because its `run_date` job parameter was wrong. An orchestration script must repair all failed tasks again, this time with `run_date` set to `2026-10-25`, through `POST /api/2.2/jobs/runs/repair`. Which request body is correct?

choices.A: `{"run_id": 455644833, "rerun_all_failed_tasks": true, "job_parameters": {"run_date": "2026-10-25"}}`
choices.B: `{"run_id": 455644833, "latest_repair_id": 734650698524280, "rerun_all_failed_tasks": true, "job_parameters": {"run_date": "2026-10-25"}}`
choices.C: `{"run_id": 455644833, "latest_repair_id": 734650698524280, "rerun_tasks": ["clean_b"], "rerun_all_failed_tasks": true}`
choices.D: `{"job_id": 11223344, "job_parameters": {"run_date": "2026-10-25"}, "only": ["clean_b"]}`

questions.shortAnswer: Option B supplies `latest_repair_id`, `rerun_all_failed_tasks`, and the `job_parameters` override.
questions.explanation: `latest_repair_id` is not needed for the first repair but must be provided on later repairs of the same run, and `job_parameters` carries the override. A omits `latest_repair_id` for a second repair. C sets both `rerun_tasks` and `rerun_all_failed_tasks`, which are mutually exclusive, and has no override. D is a `run-now` request that starts a new run instead of repairing the existing one.

questions.title: Same Definitions in Every Environment *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team wants one job and one Lakeflow pipeline, stored in Git, deployed to dev, staging, and prod workspaces with a different catalog per environment and a service principal running production. Which approach fits?

choices.A: Build the job in the dev UI, export its JSON, and import it into staging and prod
choices.B: Define the resources once in a `databricks.yml` bundle with `targets` that override a `catalog` variable and set `run_as` on `prod`, then run `databricks bundle deploy -t <target>`
choices.C: Keep the job in a Git folder and copy the folder to each workspace with the workspace import CLI
choices.D: Use one shared workspace for all three environments to avoid configuration drift

questions.shortAnswer: A Declarative Automation Bundle with per-target overrides deploys identical definitions to each environment.
questions.explanation: Bundles declare resources as code, `targets` override variables per environment, `run_as` sets a production service principal, and `databricks bundle deploy -t <target>` deploys reproducibly from CI/CD. A is manual and drifts. C moves code only, not job or pipeline definitions. D removes environment isolation instead of managing it.

questions.title: Development Mode Behavior *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: An engineer deploys a bundle with `databricks bundle deploy -t dev`, where the `dev` target sets `mode: development`. The bundle's job has a daily schedule. What does the deployed job look like?

choices.A: Same name as production, schedule active
choices.B: Name prefixed with `[dev <short_name>]`, a `dev` tag added, and the schedule paused
choices.C: Same name as production, schedule paused, and the job runs as a service principal automatically
choices.D: Deployment fails because development mode requires `run_as`

questions.shortAnswer: Development mode prefixes names, tags resources `dev`, and pauses schedules and triggers.
questions.explanation: `mode: development` prepends `[dev ${workspace.current_user.short_name}]` to resource names, adds a `dev` tag, pauses all schedules and triggers, marks pipelines as development, and disables the deployment lock. A and C keep the production name, which development mode changes. D confuses it with production mode, which is where `run_as` (a service principal) is recommended or required.

questions.title: Updating a Production Git Folder from CI *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team deploys only notebooks and Python files through a production Git folder at `/Workspace/Production/etl`. After each pull request merges into `main`, their GitHub Actions workflow must bring that folder to the latest commit of `main`. Which command should the workflow run, authenticated as a service principal that has a Git credential?

choices.A: `databricks repos update /Workspace/Production/etl --branch main`
choices.B: `databricks workspace import-dir ./src /Workspace/Production/etl --overwrite`
choices.C: `databricks repos create https://github.com/org/etl.git gitHub --path /Workspace/Production/etl`
choices.D: `databricks bundle destroy -t prod` followed by `databricks bundle deploy -t prod`

questions.shortAnswer: `databricks repos update ... --branch main` checks out `main` and pulls its latest commit into the Git folder.
questions.explanation: The Repos API update (`PATCH /api/2.0/repos/{id}`) switches a Git folder to a branch or tag or updates it to the latest commit on the same branch, which is the documented automation for a production Git folder. B bypasses Git and turns the folder's contents into untracked copies. C clones a new Git folder and fails if the path already exists. D tears down bundle resources and is unrelated to updating a Git folder.

questions.title: Git Folders vs Bundles *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team uses personal Git folders for development. They now need CI/CD that deploys both the notebook code and the job definitions (schedules, clusters, task graph) to production. What does Databricks recommend?

choices.A: A production Git folder only, because pulling the branch also updates job definitions
choices.B: Declarative Automation Bundles, with the jobs defined in source and deployed by `databricks bundle deploy`
choices.C: Editing the production jobs in the UI after each Git folder pull
choices.D: Storing job JSON in the Git folder and relying on Databricks to apply it automatically

questions.shortAnswer: Databricks recommends Declarative Automation Bundles to package and deploy CI/CD workflows.
questions.explanation: Bundles deploy code plus jobs and pipelines as code, while a production Git folder deploys code only. A is wrong because updating a Git folder does not change job definitions. C is manual and error-prone. D is wrong because Databricks does not apply job JSON files from a Git folder automatically.

questions.title: Medallion Architecture
questions.question: A data architect is designing a lakehouse. Raw JSON data needs to be ingested, cleaned, and then aggregated. In which layer should data type casting and null handling occur?

choices.A: Bronze layer
choices.B: Silver layer
choices.C: Gold layer
choices.D: Landing zone

questions.shortAnswer: The Silver layer is for cleaned, conformed data including type casting, null handling, deduplication, and standardization. Bronze stores raw data as-is. Gold is for business-level aggregations. Landing zone is temporary staging.

questions.title: Schema Evolution
questions.question: A streaming pipeline receives data with a new column. The target Delta table should automatically accept this change. Which option enables this?

choices.A: `.option("mergeSchema", "true")`
choices.B: `.option("overwriteSchema", "true")`
choices.C: `.option("schemaEvolution", "true")`
choices.D: Schema evolution is automatic in Delta

questions.shortAnswer: `mergeSchema = true` allows adding new columns during writes. `overwriteSchema` replaces the entire schema (dangerous). Option C is not a valid option. Schema evolution must be explicitly enabled.

questions.title: SCD Type 2
questions.question: A dimension table needs to track full history of changes with effective dates. Which columns are typically added for SCD Type 2?

choices.A: `is_current`, `version`
choices.B: `start_date`, `end_date`, `is_current`
choices.C: `created_at`, `updated_at`
choices.D: `previous_value`, `current_value`

questions.shortAnswer: SCD Type 2 tracks history using `start_date` (when version became active), `end_date` (when superseded, NULL for current), and often `is_current` flag. This allows point-in-time queries and current state queries.

questions.title: Partitioning Best Practices
questions.question: A table has 100 million rows with a `status` column containing 5 distinct values and a `customer_id` column with 1 million distinct values. Which partitioning strategy is correct?

choices.A: Partition by `customer_id`
choices.B: Partition by `status`
choices.C: Partition by both `customer_id` and `status`
choices.D: Don't partition, use Z-ORDER on `customer_id`

questions.shortAnswer: Partitioning works best for low-cardinality columns with ~1000 or fewer values. `customer_id` has too many values (would create 1M partitions). `status` has too few values (only 5 partitions, may not help much). Z-ORDER or liquid clustering on high-cardinality columns is better.

questions.title: One Definition, Any Grouping *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: Finance defines average order value as net revenue divided by the number of distinct orders. Analysts query it from AI/BI dashboards, Genie Agents, and Power BI, grouped by region in one report and by month and customer segment in another. Some reports currently average pre-aggregated daily ratios and get wrong numbers. Which design gives one governed definition that stays correct at any grouping?

choices.A: A Unity Catalog metric view over `fact_sales` with atomic measures for net revenue and order count, and `avg_order_value` defined as `MEASURE(net_revenue) / MEASURE(order_count)`
choices.B: A materialized view that stores average order value by day, region, and segment
choices.C: A standard view that computes `AVG(order_value)` grouped by region
choices.D: A Python UDF that each notebook imports to compute the ratio

questions.shortAnswer: A metric view defines measures once and lets consumers group by any field. The engine computes the ratio from the atomic measures at the requested grain.
questions.explanation: Metric views separate measure definitions from fields, so a composed measure like `MEASURE(net_revenue) / MEASURE(order_count)` re-aggregates correctly for any `GROUP BY` and is governed in Unity Catalog for every tool. A materialized view (B) fixes the grain, and averaging stored ratios across rows gives the wrong answer. A standard view (C) fixes its grouping and uses a different formula. A UDF copied into notebooks (D) isn't governed and doesn't reach dashboards or BI tools.

questions.title: Enabling Incremental Materialized View Refresh *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Gold materialized view, refreshed on serverless, pre-aggregates the Delta tables `fact_sales` and `dim_product` for dashboards. Neither source table has row tracking enabled. Every refresh shows a `FULL_RECOMPUTE` technique in the event log, and refresh cost keeps growing with table size. The query uses only `SUM` over `DECIMAL` columns, `GROUP BY`, and an inner join between the two tables. Which change most directly allows incremental refresh?

choices.A: Add a `customer_key BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` column to the materialized view
choices.B: Cast the `DECIMAL` amounts to `DOUBLE` before summing
choices.C: Enable row tracking on the source tables and set `REFRESH POLICY INCREMENTAL STRICT` so a non-incremental plan fails instead of recomputing
choices.D: Convert the materialized view to a standard view so it's computed at query time

questions.shortAnswer: Incremental refresh needs supported operations, serverless refresh, and row tracking on the Delta sources. `INCREMENTAL STRICT` makes any remaining blocker fail loudly instead of silently recomputing.
questions.explanation: The docs say source Delta tables should have row tracking enabled to support incremental refresh, and `REFRESH POLICY INCREMENTAL STRICT` fails the refresh rather than falling back to a full recompute. That makes the cause visible and stops the cost growth. Materialized views don't support identity columns or surrogate keys (A). `SUM` over `FLOAT` or `DOUBLE` forces a full refresh, so casting to `DOUBLE` (B) makes things worse. A standard view (D) removes the pre-computation the dashboards depend on.

questions.title: Fixing an Over-Partitioned Table *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A 600 GB Delta table is partitioned by `customer_id` and has millions of small files. Queries filter on `customer_id` and on `event_date`. The workspace runs Databricks Runtime 18.1. The engineer wants better data skipping and balanced file sizes without a manual CTAS rebuild. What should the engineer do?

choices.A: Add a generated `event_month` column and repartition the table by `(event_month, customer_id)`
choices.B: Keep the partitions and run `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (event_date)` in each partition
choices.C: Lower `delta.targetFileSize` to 16 MB so each partition writes smaller files
choices.D: Run `ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY (customer_id, event_date)` and then `OPTIMIZE`

questions.shortAnswer: Converting in place to liquid clustering on the filter columns, then running `OPTIMIZE`, fixes both data skipping and file sizes.
questions.explanation: The docs say not to partition tables under 1 TB at all, and partitioning by a high-cardinality column creates the small-file problem described here. In DBR 18.1+, `REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY` converts the table without a full manual rebuild, and `OPTIMIZE` then clusters and compacts the data. Option A keeps a partitioned layout below the recommended size and still partitions on a high-cardinality column. Option B leaves millions of small partitions in place, because Z-order can't combine files across partition boundaries. Option C makes the small-file problem worse.

questions.title: Clustering a Fact Table for Star-Schema Joins *(2026 blueprint)*
questions.question: A 30 TB unpartitioned fact table, `fact_sales`, is joined to a small filtered `dim_product` table on `product_key`, and most queries also filter on `sale_date`. Query profiles show that dynamic file pruning is applied but still scans most fact files, because `product_key` values are spread across every file. Which layout change best aligns the table with this access pattern?

choices.A: Partition `fact_sales` by `product_key`
choices.B: Enable liquid clustering on `fact_sales` with `CLUSTER BY (sale_date, product_key)`, then run `OPTIMIZE ... FULL`
choices.C: Set `delta.targetFileSize` to 32 MB so there are more files to skip
choices.D: Disable predictive optimization and schedule `VACUUM` every hour

questions.shortAnswer: Liquid clustering on the filter column and the join key puts matching rows in fewer files, so dynamic file pruning can skip more of them. `OPTIMIZE FULL` reclusters the existing data.
questions.explanation: The dynamic file pruning docs say its effect depends on how data is clustered, and recommend liquid clustering on frequently joined columns. Clustering keys should come from the most common filter and join columns, up to four keys. Partitioning on a high-cardinality join key (A) causes over-partitioning and small files, and the docs prefer liquid clustering below 100 TB anyway. Shrinking files (C) works against the autotuned 1 GB target for a table this size and adds metadata overhead. `VACUUM` (D) removes unreferenced files and doesn't change data layout.
